LangChain + Ollama
ChromaDB & RAG

Build a question-answering app that runs on your own machine: Llama 3.2 served by Ollama, your documents stored in ChromaDB, LangChain joining them, FastAPI exposing it, and an Angular chat page that calls it. For each file you read the full code, then practise it part by part, and the page checks your lines against the original. You finish with an agent that can call tools, and a set of interview questions. Use the tabs at the top of the page to choose a track: Ollama runs the model on your machine, OpenRouter reaches many hosted models with one key, vLLM serves open models from your own GPU server, and Claude and ChatGPT call Anthropic or OpenAI directly, with your key kept in a .env file. The Git tab shows how to put the finished project on GitHub.

What you will have at the end: a project folder with a handful of small Python files, plus an Angular app next to it. vectordb.py opens your ChromaDB collection, rag.py answers questions from it, main.py exposes POST /ask and POST /add, the Angular chat page calls them, and tools.py lets the model ask your code to run functions.

You need Python 3.10 or newer, Ollama installed, a current Node.js LTS for Angular (Angular CLI 20 or newer), and some comfort with the terminal. In the practice boxes, Tab adds spaces and Enter keeps your indent. To move focus out of a box with the keyboard, press Esc, then Tab.

Step 1 Understand how it all works

Embeddings: an embedding model (nomic-embed-text) turns a piece of text into a list of numbers. Texts with similar meaning get similar numbers.
ChromaDB: stores each chunk of text together with its numbers. When you search, your question becomes numbers too, and Chroma returns the chunks that are closest.
RAG: you paste those chunks into the prompt and ask Llama to answer only from them, so answers come from your documents.
FastAPI: wraps all of this in HTTP endpoints, so your Angular app can call POST /ask.

Question
↓
Retriever (LangChain)
↓
ChromaDB returns the closest chunks
↓
Prompt = chunks + question
↓
Llama 3.2 (Ollama)
↓
Answer

Step 2 Install the tools

Install Ollama from ollama.com and keep it running. Then create a new folder for the project and work inside it. Every file in this guide goes in that folder.

Install the Python packages

LangChain is split into small packages. langchain is the core. langchain-ollama and langchain-chroma connect it to Ollama and ChromaDB. langchain-text-splitters cuts long text into chunks. fastapi and uvicorn are the web framework and its server.

Read the command

Practise it

Install the packages

Use one pip install command for langchain, langchain-ollama, langchain-chroma, langchain-text-splitters, fastapi and uvicorn, in that order. Write it here, then run it in your terminal.

Download the two models

llama3.2:3b writes the answers. The :3b after the colon is the tag that picks the 3-billion-parameter version, which is small enough for most laptops. Writing ollama pull llama3.2 with no tag downloads the same model by default, but this guide writes the tag so the name in your code matches exactly. nomic-embed-text makes the embeddings. You only pull each model once. While you work, Ollama must be running, either as the desktop app or with ollama serve in a spare terminal.

Read the commands

Practise it

Pull both models

Write the two ollama pull commands, one per line: first the chat model, then the embedding model.

Step 3 Talk to Llama from LangChain

chat.py

Create a new, empty chat.py. It sends one question to the model and prints the answer.

ChatOllama is LangChain's wrapper around a local Ollama model. invoke() returns a message object, not a plain string, so you read the text from .content. Run it with python chat.py.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Write the import

Import ChatOllama from langchain_ollama.

Create the model

Create a variable llm by calling ChatOllama with model="llama3.2:3b".

Ask and print

Call llm.invoke() with "What is RBAC?" and keep the result in response. Then print response.content.

chat.py · use a reusable prompt

Keep working in the same chat.py. In this part we are going to change it. Instead of typing the question straight into the code, we will use a reusable prompt. So the two lines that asked "What is RBAC?" directly are replaced, and you do not need both ways.

What you already wrote

A PromptTemplate is text with {placeholders}. Joining it to the model with | makes a chain. You call the chain with a dict whose keys match the placeholder names, so the key topic must match {topic} exactly. The two old lines that called llm.invoke() directly are gone, because the chain does that job now. Run it with python chat.py and you will see one answer: a one-sentence explanation of RBAC. Change "RBAC" to another topic and run it again to see the template reused.

Full code after your changes

Right now the question "What is RBAC?" is typed straight into the code. A PromptTemplate lets you write the question once with a blank like {topic} and fill in any topic later. Think of it as a printed form with a blank, instead of a handwritten note.

Practise the lines you change

Add the import

At the top of the file, add one new import: import PromptTemplate from langchain_core.prompts.

Replace the direct question with a prompt and a chain

The box shows the two old lines that asked the question directly. Delete them and write this instead: create prompt with PromptTemplate.from_template() and the text "Explain {topic} in one sentence.". Then create chain by joining prompt and llm with |. You keep the same llm.

Run the chain

Still at the bottom: call chain.invoke() with a dict that sets "topic" to "RBAC", and keep the result in result. Then print result.content.

chatbot.py

Create a new, empty chatbot.py. This is a separate small program, so it sets up the model again. A chatbot is a loop: read a question, call the model, print the answer. This one has no memory, so every question is answered on its own.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Set up the model

Import ChatOllama from langchain_ollama, then create llm with model="llama3.2:3b".

Read questions until the user quits

Write a while True: loop. Inside it, read a line with input("You: ") into question. If question equals "exit", break.

Answer each question

Still inside the loop, after the if: call llm.invoke(question) into answer, then print "Bot:" and answer.content.

Step 4 Turn text into numbers

embed.py

Create a new, empty embed.py. You rarely call embeddings yourself, because ChromaDB does it for you. Doing it once makes it less mysterious.

Use embed_query for one search question and embed_documents for a list of texts you want to store. Always use the same embedding model for adding and searching, or the results are meaningless.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Create the embedding model

Import OllamaEmbeddings from langchain_ollama. Create embeddings with model="nomic-embed-text".

Embed one question

Call embeddings.embed_query() with "What is RBAC?" into vector, then print how long vector is.

Embed a list of texts

Make a list texts holding the two strings "RBAC stands for Role-Based Access Control." and "FastAPI is a Python web framework.", one per line. Pass it to embed_documents() to get vectors, and print how many vectors there are.

Step 5 Store and search with ChromaDB

You open the database once, in its own file, and import it everywhere else. That way every script uses the same collection and the same embedding model.

vectordb.py

Create a new, empty vectordb.py.

Without persist_directory, everything lives in memory and disappears when the script ends. The folder chroma_db is created for you.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Write the imports

Import Chroma from langchain_chroma and OllamaEmbeddings from langchain_ollama.

Create the embedding model

Create embeddings with OllamaEmbeddings and model="nomic-embed-text".

Open the collection

Create db by calling Chroma( with one argument per line: collection_name="my_docs", persist_directory="chroma_db" and embedding_function=embeddings. Close the call with ) on its own line.

quick_add.py

Create a new, empty quick_add.py. It stores two short texts, which is the fastest way to get something into the database.

metadatas is optional but useful: you can filter searches by it and show where an answer came from. Because ids are stable, re-running the script updates the entries instead of creating duplicates.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Import the database

Import db from vectordb.

Add two texts

Call db.add_texts( with one argument per line. texts is a list of the two strings (each on its own line). metadatas is [{"source": "security.md"}, {"source": "fastapi.md"}]. ids is ["doc1", "doc2"]. Close with ) on its own line.

ingest.py

Create a new, empty ingest.py, and put a text file called notes.txt next to it. This script loads a real file into the database.

Embeddings work best on small pieces of text, and a search returns chunks, not whole files. chunk_size is characters per chunk. chunk_overlap repeats a little text between neighbours, so a sentence isn't cut off from its context. Around 300 to 800 characters is a good start.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Write the imports

Import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter from langchain_text_splitters, and db from vectordb.

Read the file

Open "notes.txt" with encoding="utf-8" using a with block, as f. Inside it, read the whole file with f.read() into text.

Split it into chunks

Create splitter from RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter with chunk_size=500 and chunk_overlap=50. Then create chunks with splitter.create_documents(), passing [text] and metadatas=[{"source": "notes.txt"}].

Store the chunks

Add the chunks with db.add_documents(). Then print an f-string: Added, the number of chunks, and chunks.

ingest.py · read a PDF instead

Keep working in the same ingest.py. Many real documents are PDFs, not text files. In this part we change the script so it reads notes.pdf and not notes.txt. Put a PDF called notes.pdf next to the script, and install the reader first with pip install PyPDF2.

What you already wrote

The old with open(...) block is gone, because PdfReader opens the file itself. The source in the metadata now says notes.pdf, so a search filter or an answer can show where the text came from. Testing the reader alone? Add print(text) after the loop to see the extracted text, then remove it. Limits: a scanned PDF is just pictures, so extract_text() returns nothing and you would need OCR. PyPDF2 is no longer developed. Its maintained successor is pypdf, which works the same way with from pypdf import PdfReader.

Full code after your changes

A text file can be read with one read() call, but a PDF is a list of pages. PdfReader opens the file, reader.pages gives you the pages, and extract_text() pulls the text out of one page. You join every page into one string, so everything after that line (the splitter and the database) stays exactly the same.

Practise the lines you change

Add the PDF import

At the top of the file, add one new import: import PdfReader from PyPDF2.

Read the PDF instead of the text file

The box shows the old lines that read notes.txt. Delete them and write this instead: create reader from PdfReader("notes.pdf"). Then set text to an empty string. Then loop over reader.pages as page, and add page.extract_text() to text with +=.

Update the source name

The box shows the old chunks line. Rewrite it so the metadata says {"source": "notes.pdf"} instead of notes.txt.

similarity_search embeds your question and returns the stored chunks with the closest meaning. k is how many to return. filter keeps only entries whose metadata matches. Each result is a Document.

Print each result

Loop over results as doc. Print doc.page_content, then doc.metadata.

Step 6 Answer questions from your documents (RAG)

rag.py

Create a new, empty rag.py. This is the heart of the project: retrieve the right chunks, paste them into the prompt, and ask Llama to answer only from them.

Telling the model to answer only from the context, and to admit when the answer is missing, is what keeps it from making things up. The if __name__ == "__main__": block runs only when you run python rag.py directly. When another file imports ask, it is skipped.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Write the imports

Import ChatOllama from langchain_ollama and db from vectordb.

Make the retriever and the model

Create retriever with db.as_retriever() and search_kwargs={"k": 3}. Create llm with ChatOllama and model="llama3.2:3b".

Retrieve the context

Define ask(question: str) -> str. Inside it, call retriever.invoke(question) into docs. Then build context by joining every d.page_content in docs with "\n\n".

Build the prompt

Inside ask(), create prompt as three or more string pieces inside parentheses, one piece per line. The first two lines are "Answer using only the context below. " and "If the answer is not in the context, say you do not know.\n\n". Then add the f-strings f"Context:\n{context}\n\n" and f"Question: {question}". Close with ) on its own line.

Return the answer

Last line of ask(): return the .content of llm.invoke(prompt).

Try it from the terminal

At the left edge, write if __name__ == "__main__":. Inside it, print the result of ask("What is RBAC?").

Step 7 Expose it with FastAPI

Your Angular app can't import Python. It talks to HTTP endpoints, so this file turns ask() and the database into POST /ask and POST /add.

main.py

Create a new, empty main.py.

body: Question tells FastAPI to read the JSON body and check that it has a question string. If something is missing, FastAPI answers with a 422 error before your code runs. The endpoint is called ask_endpoint so it doesn't hide the ask function you imported.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Write the imports

Import FastAPI from fastapi, CORSMiddleware from fastapi.middleware.cors, BaseModel from pydantic, db from vectordb, and ask from rag. One import per line, in that order.

Create the app

Create a variable called app by calling FastAPI().

Let Angular call the API

Call app.add_middleware() with CORSMiddleware, one argument per line. Set allow_origins to a list holding "http://localhost:4200", and set allow_methods and allow_headers to ["*"].

Describe the /ask body

Write a class Question that extends BaseModel, with one str field: question.

Describe the /add body

Write a class Doc that extends BaseModel, with a str field text and a str field source whose default value is "api".

Write the /ask route

Add @app.post("/ask"). Below it, define ask_endpoint(body: Question). It returns a dict with the key "answer" and the value ask(body.question).

Write the /add route

Add @app.post("/add") and define add(doc: Doc). Inside it, call db.add_texts() with a list holding doc.text and metadatas=[{"source": doc.source}]. Return {"status": "added"}.

Run the backend

main:app means "the app variable inside main.py". --reload restarts the server whenever you save. It listens on port 8000 unless you add --port. Leave this terminal open while you test Angular.

Open http://localhost:8000/docs in your browser. FastAPI builds a page there where you can try /add and /ask before Angular exists.

Run the server

What the CLI already wrote

The component holds the screen state: what is typed, whether it is waiting, and the list of messages. It never touches HTTP. subscribe takes an object with next for a good reply and error for a failed request, so the page can show a message instead of hanging.

Full code after your changes

Update the imports

The box has the import the CLI wrote. Add inject to it. Then import FormsModule from @angular/forms, and ApiService from ../service/api.service.

Describe a message

Under the imports, write an interface Message with two fields: from, which is either 'you' or 'bot', and text, a string.

Let the template use ngModel

The box has the empty imports array from the decorator. Put FormsModule inside it.

Inject the service and add the state

Inside the class, add a private field api set to inject(ApiService). Then add question starting as '', loading starting as false, and messages, an empty array typed Message[].

Start send()

Write send(). Read this.question.trim() into const text. If text is empty or this.loading is true, return. Then push { from: 'you', text } onto this.messages, clear this.question to '', and set this.loading to true.

Call the backend

Inside send(), before its closing }, call this.api.ask(text).subscribe() with an object. Its next handler takes res, pushes { from: 'bot', text: res.answer }, and sets loading to false. Its error handler pushes a bot message with the text 'Sorry, something went wrong.' and also sets loading to false.

Step 9 Give the model tools

So far the pipeline is fixed: always retrieve, then answer. An agent decides for itself whether it needs a tool. A tool is just a Python function the model is allowed to ask for. The model never runs it. It replies with the tool's name and arguments, and your code runs the function.

tools.py

Create a new, empty tools.py.

The docstring matters: it is how the model learns what a tool does and when to use it. In a full agent you would send each result back to the model so it can write the final answer. Here you stop at running the call yourself, which is the part to understand first.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Write the imports

Import tool from langchain_core.tools, ChatOllama from langchain_ollama, and db from vectordb.

Make the retriever

Create retriever with db.as_retriever() and search_kwargs={"k": 3}.

Define the add tool

Decorate a function with @tool. Define add(a: int, b: int) -> int. Give it the one-line docstring """Add two integers and return the sum.""" and make it return a + b.

Define the search tool

Decorate search_docs(query: str) -> str with @tool. Its docstring is """Search the knowledge base for passages relevant to the query.""". Inside, call retriever.invoke(query) into docs, and return the page_content of every doc joined with "\n\n".

List the tools

Create tools as a list holding add and search_docs. Create tools_by_name as a dict comprehension mapping t.name to t for each t in tools.

Show the model its tools

Create llm with ChatOllama and model="llama3.2:3b". Then create llm_with_tools with llm.bind_tools(tools).

Ask a question that needs a tool

Call llm_with_tools.invoke() with "What is 3 + 4?" into response. Print response.tool_calls.

Run each tool call yourself

Loop over response.tool_calls as call. Inside, look up the tool with tools_by_name[call["name"]] and call its invoke() with call["args"], keeping the result in result. Print call["name"], the text "->", and result.

Step 10 Put it all together

You have written many small files, and a working app needs only some of them. This step shows which ones, how they find each other, and how to start everything in the right order.

The smallest working project

Four Python files make the whole backend: vectordb.py, rag.py, main.py and ingest.py. Add notes.txt for your documents, and the Angular app, and you have the full product. Everything else is optional. This is how the folder looks when it is complete.

rag-app/
├── vectordb.py         opens the ChromaDB collection
├── rag.py              ask(): retrieve, build the prompt, call the model
├── main.py             FastAPI app with POST /ask and POST /add
├── ingest.py           loads notes.txt into the database
├── try_api.py          calls the running API from Python
├── notes.txt           your documents
├── requirements.txt    the packages to install
├── .venv/              your virtual environment (made by Python)
├── chroma_db/          the stored vectors (made by ChromaDB)
└── frontend/           the Angular app from Step 8

main.pyThe web app. It exposes /ask and /add.rag.py, vectordb.py

Python finds from vectordb import db by looking for a file called vectordb.py in the folder you run from. The files must sit side by side, and each file name must match its import name exactly. The learning scripts, chat.py, chain.py, chatbot.py, embed.py, quick_add.py, search.py, manage.py and tools.py, are not needed to run the app. Keep them beside the others if you want to run them. quick_add.py, search.py, manage.py and tools.py import vectordb.py, so they stop working if you move them into a subfolder.

Test the API from Python

The /docs page is good for a first try. A small script is better, because you can run it again after every change.

try_api.py

Create a new, empty try_api.py. It calls your running FastAPI server the same way Angular does: it adds one sentence with /add, then asks about it with /ask.

requests.post() sends an HTTP POST. Passing json= turns the dict into a JSON body and sets the right header, which matches the Doc and Question models in main.py. A status of 200 means it worked. Every run adds the demo sentence again, which is harmless for a test.

Start everything in order

The order matters, because each step needs the one before it. You will have two or three terminals open.

  1. Start Ollama, either the desktop app or ollama serve.
  2. Open a terminal in the project folder and activate the environment.
  3. Run python ingest.py. Run it again only when notes.txt changes.
  4. Run uvicorn main:app --reload and leave this terminal open.
  5. Open a second terminal in the project folder, activate the environment, and run python try_api.py. You should see 200 and a reply.
  6. Open a third terminal in the frontend folder and run ng serve. Then open http://localhost:4200.

You built the whole pipeline

Documents in, grounded answers out

You can now store text in ChromaDB, retrieve the closest chunks, hand them to Llama as context, expose the result over HTTP, and let the model ask for tools. Good next steps are chat history so follow-up questions work, streaming the answer token by token, and adding more sources with metadata filters.

Interview questions

Try to answer each one aloud before you open it.

What is RAG, and why use it?

Retrieval-augmented generation finds the pieces of your own documents that match a question and puts them in the prompt. The model then answers from that text. It lets a general model answer about private or recent data without retraining it, and it cuts down on made-up answers.

What is an embedding?

A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Texts with similar meaning get vectors that are close together, which is what makes similarity search possible.

Why split documents into chunks?

A search returns whole chunks, and embeddings represent a single focused idea better than a long file. Chunks that are too big give vague matches. Chunks that are too small lose context.

What does chunk_overlap do?

It repeats a little text at the edges of neighbouring chunks, so a sentence or idea that falls on a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk.

Why must you use the same embedding model for storing and searching?

Each model produces its own kind of vectors. Vectors from different models aren't comparable, and they may even have different lengths, so searches return nonsense or fail with a dimension error.

What is the difference between similarity_search and a retriever?

similarity_search is a method on the database that returns documents. A retriever is a standard wrapper around a search with an invoke() method, so chains, agents and tools can all call it the same way.

Why do the HTTP calls live in a service and not in the component?

The component should be about the screen: what is typed and what is shown. A service keeps the URL and the request shape in one place, so if the API changes you fix one file, and components stay easy to read and test.

What does provideHttpClient() do?

It registers HttpClient in the app's injector, so any service or component can ask for it with inject(HttpClient). Without it, Angular throws NullInjectorError: No provider for HttpClient.

Why does the browser need CORS to be set up?

Angular on port 4200 and FastAPI on port 8000 are different origins. Browsers block such calls unless the server says that origin is allowed, which is what CORSMiddleware with allow_origins does.

Why does python main.py not start the server?

main.py only creates the app object and its routes. A server such as uvicorn has to load that file and listen for requests, which is why you run uvicorn main:app --reload instead.

Why keep a requirements.txt and a virtual environment?

The virtual environment gives the project its own set of packages, so versions don't clash with other projects. requirements.txt records what to install, so anyone can rebuild the same setup with pip install -r requirements.txt.

Does the model run a tool itself?

No. With tools bound, the model replies with a tool call: the tool's name and the arguments it wants. Your code runs the function and, in a full agent, sends the result back so the model can write the final answer.

The same app, with the model in the cloud. OpenRouter is one API that reaches many hosted models. It speaks the same protocol as OpenAI, so LangChain talks to it with ChatOpenAI and OpenAIEmbeddings, pointed at OpenRouter's address. You need no Ollama and no model downloads. Your key lives in a .env file, and one small file, config.py, builds the model objects that every other file imports.

The files quick_add.py, ingest.py, search.py, manage.py, main.py and the whole Angular step are identical to the Ollama tab, so copy them over from there. This tab covers every file that changes.

Step 1 What changes with OpenRouter

Chat model: a hosted model such as openai/gpt-4o-mini instead of llama3.2:3b on your machine.
Embeddings: OpenRouter also serves embedding models, for example openai/text-embedding-3-small, so nothing runs locally.
Secrets: the API key goes in .env and is read with python-dotenv. It never goes in your code, in git, or in Angular.

Question
↓
Retriever (LangChain)
↓
ChromaDB returns the closest chunks
↓
Prompt = chunks + question
↓
Model on OpenRouter (key from .env)
↓
Answer
Keep the key on the backend. Anything in Angular is visible to every visitor. Only your Python server reads .env, and Angular calls your FastAPI endpoints, never OpenRouter directly. Also, calls to paid models use your OpenRouter credits, so keep an eye on your usage.
Never type your real key into this page. The boxes below save your text in your browser. Where a box needs the key, type the placeholder shown. Put the real key only in the .env file on your own machine.

Step 2 Get a key and set up the project

Create an account at openrouter.ai, then create an API key under your account's keys page. Make a new project folder, or reuse the one from the Ollama tab. The files below go in that folder.

Install the Python packages

langchain-openai replaces langchain-ollama. It provides ChatOpenAI and OpenAIEmbeddings, which work with any server that speaks the OpenAI protocol. python-dotenv reads your .env file.

.env

Create a file named exactly .env in your project folder, next to the config.py you will write in Step 3. Python looks for it there, and in the folders above it, but not in other places.

Each line is NAME=value, with no spaces around the = and no quotes. In your real file, replace sk-or-v1-your-key-here with your key. The two model lines let you switch models without touching Python. You can browse model names on openrouter.ai/models, and a model's page shows its exact ID.

Write the three settings

.gitignore

If this folder is a git repository, tell git to never track the secret file.

The first line is the important one. A key that reaches GitHub can be found and used by anyone, so if that ever happens, delete the key on OpenRouter and make a new one. The other lines skip the virtual environment, the database folders and Python's cache.

config.py

Create a new, empty config.py.

base_url is the key idea: it points the OpenAI client at OpenRouter instead of at OpenAI. os.getenv(name, default) returns the environment variable, or the default when it isn't set. Stopping with a clear error when the key is missing saves you from a confusing failure later. check_embedding_ctx_length=False is needed because the client would otherwise turn your text into OpenAI-specific token numbers before sending it.

Step 9 Give the model tools

tools.py

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Write the imports

Import tool from langchain_core.tools, llm from config, and db from vectordb.

Make the retriever

Create retriever with db.as_retriever() and search_kwargs={"k": 3}.

Define the add tool

Decorate a function with @tool. Define add(a: int, b: int) -> int. Give it the one-line docstring """Add two integers and return the sum.""" and make it return a + b.

Define the search tool

Decorate search_docs(query: str) -> str with @tool. Its docstring is """Search the knowledge base for passages relevant to the query.""". Inside, call retriever.invoke(query) into docs, and return the page_content of every doc joined with "\n\n".

List the tools

Create tools as a list holding add and search_docs. Create tools_by_name as a dict comprehension mapping t.name to t for each t in tools.

Show the model its tools

Create llm_with_tools with llm.bind_tools(tools).

Ask a question that needs a tool

Call llm_with_tools.invoke() with "What is 3 + 4?" into response. Print response.tool_calls.

Run each tool call yourself

Loop over response.tool_calls as call. Inside, look up the tool with tools_by_name[call["name"]] and call its invoke() with call["args"], keeping the result in result. Print call["name"], the text "->", and result.

Step 10 Put it all together

You have written many small files, and a working app needs only some of them. This step shows which ones, how they find each other, and how to start everything in the right order.

The smallest working project

Five Python files and a .env file make the whole backend: config.py, vectordb.py, rag.py, main.py and ingest.py. main.py and ingest.py are the same files as in the Ollama tab. Add notes.txt for your documents, and the Angular app, and you have the full product. This is how the folder looks when it is complete.

Same app, hosted model

Secrets out of the code, one file to swap providers

You now have the whole pipeline running on a hosted model, with the key kept in .env and read by config.py. Because every file imports llm and embeddings from one place, moving to another model, or back to Ollama, means editing only config.py and its .env.

Interview questions

Try to answer each one aloud before you open it.

Why keep an API key in a .env file?

It keeps secrets out of your source code and out of git. The code only reads an environment variable, so each machine or server can have its own key, and you can change a key without editing any code.

Why can't the API key live in the Angular app?

Everything sent to the browser can be read by anyone who opens the developer tools. A key there can be copied and used on your account. The key stays on the backend, and Angular only calls your own endpoints.

What does base_url do in ChatOpenAI?

It points the OpenAI client at a different server. OpenRouter accepts the same requests as OpenAI, so changing the address and the key is enough to use its models.

What does load_dotenv() do?

It reads the NAME=value lines of the .env file and adds them to the process's environment variables, so os.getenv can find them.

Why use a separate Chroma folder after switching embedding models?

Each embedding model makes vectors of its own length, and vectors from different models can't be compared. A collection that already holds one length rejects the other, so use a new folder or re-ingest everything with the new model.

Where does load_dotenv() look for the .env file?

It starts in the folder of the file that calls it, here config.py, and walks up through the parent folders. So .env belongs next to config.py, and it is found no matter which folder you run the server from.

Why does python main.py not start the server?

main.py only creates the app object and its routes. A server such as uvicorn has to load that file and listen for requests, which is why you run uvicorn main:app --reload instead.

What is OpenRouter?

A service with a single API that routes your request to many hosted models from different providers. You change the model by changing its name, not your integration code.

The same app, with the model served by vLLM. vLLM is a fast inference server that you run yourself. It loads a model from Hugging Face and exposes the OpenAI protocol, so LangChain talks to it with ChatOpenAI and OpenAIEmbeddings, pointed at your own address. There is no Ollama and no API key. Like the OpenRouter tab, one file, config.py, builds the model objects that every other file imports.

Check your hardware first. vLLM is built for Linux with an NVIDIA GPU, and the model must fit in the GPU's memory. It does not run well on a laptop without a GPU. If you have no GPU, use the Ollama tab for local models or the OpenRouter tab for hosted ones.

The files quick_add.py, ingest.py, search.py, manage.py, main.py and the whole Angular step are identical to the Ollama tab. chatbot.py, embed.py, rag.py and tools.py are identical to the OpenRouter tab, because they only import llm and embeddings from config.py. Copy them over from those tabs. This tab covers every file that changes.

Step 1 What changes with vLLM

Chat model: an open model such as Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, loaded by a vLLM server on port 8001.
Embeddings: a second vLLM server, on port 8002, running an embedding model such as BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5. One vLLM server runs one model, so chat and embeddings need two servers.
No key: your servers don't check one, so nothing secret is needed. Keep them on your own machine and don't expose the ports to the internet.

Your FastAPI backend already uses port 8000, so the vLLM servers use 8001 and 8002. Both servers are the "model" part of the diagram. Angular still only calls your own /ask and /add endpoints.

Read the command

The backend is the same five Python files as in the OpenRouter tab, without the .env file: config.py, vectordb.py, rag.py, main.py and ingest.py. Add notes.txt and the Angular app, and you have the full product. The folder looks like this when it is complete.

requirements.txt for this tab lists langchain, langchain-openai, langchain-chroma, langchain-text-splitters, fastapi, uvicorn and requests. Leave vllm out of it, and install vLLM in its own environment as in Step 2. try_api.py is the same script as in the other tabs.

Start everything in order

The order matters, because each step needs the one before it. You will have four or five terminals open.

  1. In the vLLM environment, start the chat server from Step 2. Wait until it prints that the application startup is complete.
  2. In a second terminal, start the embedding server and wait in the same way.
  3. Open a terminal in the project folder, activate the app environment, and run python chat.py. You should get an answer.
  4. Run python ingest.py. Run it again only when notes.txt changes.
  5. Run uvicorn main:app --reload and leave this terminal open.
  6. In another terminal, run python try_api.py. You should see 200 and a reply.
  7. In the frontend folder run ng serve, then open http://localhost:4200.

Step 7 Run it and check it works

  • Check that both servers answer. Open http://localhost:8001/v1/models and http://localhost:8002/v1/models in your browser. Each should list its model.
  • Run python chat.py for one answer from your own model.
  • Run python embed.py. The vector length should be 384.
  • Run python ingest.py, then python rag.py.
  • Run python tools.py. The model should ask for the add tool with a and b set to 3 and 4.

If something fails

What you seeWhyFix
Connection error / connection refusedThe vLLM server isn't running yet, or it is still loading the model.Start it, wait for the startup message, and check the port in config.py.
404, model does not existThe model name in config.py differs from the name given to vllm serve.Copy the name from http://localhost:8001/v1/models.
CUDA out of memoryThe model plus the other server don't fit in the GPU.Lower --gpu-memory-utilization, add --max-model-len 4096, or pick a smaller model.
401 or "gated repo" when the model downloadsThe model needs you to accept its license on Hugging Face.Accept the license, log in with huggingface-cli login, or choose an open model like Qwen.
Error that the model doesn't support embeddingsThe model on port 8002 is a chat model, not an embedding model.Serve an embedding model such as BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5.
Embedding dimension does not matchThe database folder holds vectors from a different embedding model.Use chroma_db_vllm as in this tab, or delete the folder and ingest again.
Tool call list is empty, or an error about tool choiceThe chat server was started without the tool flags, or the model can't call tools.Restart with --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser hermes.
Address already in useAnother program uses the port. Port 8000 belongs to FastAPI.Stop it, or change the port in the command and in config.py.
Same app, your own inference server

No third party, one file to swap providers

You now run the whole pipeline on models you serve yourself. Because every file imports llm and embeddings from config.py, moving between Ollama, OpenRouter and vLLM means editing only that file and the database folder name.

Interview questions

Try to answer each one aloud before you open it.

What is vLLM, and why use it?

An inference server that loads a model and serves it quickly to many users at once, using memory-efficient techniques such as paged attention and continuous batching. You use it when you want to host open models yourself with high throughput.

How is vLLM different from Ollama?

Ollama is built for easy local use, with one-command model downloads. vLLM is built for throughput on a GPU server, and it serves many requests at once. Both can be reached from LangChain, and vLLM does it through the OpenAI protocol.

Why can ChatOpenAI talk to vLLM?

vLLM exposes the same HTTP routes as OpenAI, such as /v1/chat/completions and /v1/embeddings. Pointing base_url at your server is enough, and the key is only a placeholder.

Why are there two vLLM servers?

One vLLM server loads one model. The chat model and the embedding model are different models, so each gets its own server and port, and each gets a share of the GPU memory.

What does --gpu-memory-utilization do?

It sets the fraction of GPU memory a server may claim. Lowering it leaves room for another model on the same GPU, but too low a value leaves no room for the model and its cache.

Why do tool calls need extra flags?

The server has to turn the model's tool-call text into structured calls. --enable-auto-tool-choice turns that on and --tool-call-parser names the format the model uses.

Why use a new Chroma folder for this setup?

Each embedding model makes vectors of its own length, and a collection rejects vectors of a different length. Here the vectors have 384 numbers, so they need their own folder or a full re-ingest.

Why does the model name in config.py have to match vllm serve?

The server registers the model under the name you gave it, and each request names the model it wants. A different name gets a 404 because the server has no model with that name.

The same app, with Claude as the chat model. LangChain reaches Anthropic's models through ChatAnthropic, with your key kept in a .env file and read by python-dotenv. One thing differs from the other hosted tabs: Anthropic has no embeddings API, so the vectors come from a small open model that runs on your own machine through langchain-huggingface. One small file, config.py, builds llm and embeddings, and every other file imports them.

This tab holds every backend file, from the database to FastAPI. Only quick_add.py, search.py, manage.py and the whole Angular step are identical to the Ollama tab, so copy those over from there. They all do from vectordb import db and work as they are.

Step 1 What changes with Claude

Chat model: a Claude model such as claude-sonnet-5-5, named in .env so you can switch without touching Python. Model names are retired over time (older ones such as claude-3-5-sonnet-latest no longer work), so check Anthropic's model list and put a current name in .env.
Embeddings: sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 runs locally and makes vectors of 384 numbers. It needs no key and costs nothing. The first run downloads about 90 MB.
Secrets: the API key goes in .env and is read with python-dotenv. It never goes in your code, in git, or in Angular.

↓

↓
ChromaDB returns the closest chunks
↓
Prompt = chunks + question
↓
Claude via ChatAnthropic (key from .env)
↓
Answer
Keep the key on the backend. Anything in Angular is visible to every visitor. Only your Python server reads .env, and Angular calls your FastAPI endpoints, never Anthropic directly. Calls to the model use your paid credits, so keep an eye on your usage.
Never type your real key into this page. The boxes below save your text in your browser. Where a box needs the key, type the placeholder shown. Put the real key only in the .env file on your own machine.

chat.py · use a reusable prompt

Keep working in the same chat.py. In this part we are going to change it. Instead of typing the question straight into the code, we will use a reusable prompt. So the two lines that asked "What is RBAC?" directly are replaced, and you do not need both ways.

What you already wrote

A PromptTemplate is text with {placeholders}. Joining it to the model with | makes a chain. You call the chain with a dict whose keys match the placeholder names, so the key topic must match {topic} exactly. The two old lines that called llm.invoke() directly are gone, because the chain does that job now. Run it with python chat.py and you will see one answer: a one-sentence explanation of RBAC. Change "RBAC" to another topic and run it again to see the template reused.

Full code after your changes

Right now the question "What is RBAC?" is typed straight into the code. A PromptTemplate lets you write the question once with a blank like {topic} and fill in any topic later. Think of it as a printed form with a blank, instead of a handwritten note.

Practise the lines you change

Add the import

At the top of the file, add one new import: import PromptTemplate from langchain_core.prompts.

Replace the direct question with a prompt and a chain

The box shows the two old lines that asked the question directly. Delete them and write this instead: create prompt with PromptTemplate.from_template() and the text "Explain {topic} in one sentence.". Then create chain by joining prompt and llm with |. You keep the same llm.

Still at the bottom: call chain.invoke() with a dict that sets "topic" to "RBAC", and keep the result in result. Then print result.content.

Create a new, empty ingest.py, and put a text file called notes.txt next to it. This script loads a real file into the database.

Embeddings work best on small pieces of text, and a search returns chunks, not whole files. chunk_size is characters per chunk. chunk_overlap repeats a little text between neighbours, so a sentence isn't cut off from its context. Around 300 to 800 characters is a good start.

Split it into chunks

Store the chunks

Your Angular app can't import Python. It talks to HTTP endpoints, so this file turns ask() and the database into POST /ask and POST /add. It is the same main.py as in the other tabs, because it only imports ask and db.

main.py

Create a new, empty main.py.

body: Question tells FastAPI to read the JSON body and check that it has a question string. If something is missing, FastAPI answers with a 422 error before your code runs. The endpoint is called ask_endpoint so it doesn't hide the ask function you imported.

Write the imports

Import FastAPI from fastapi, CORSMiddleware from fastapi.middleware.cors, BaseModel from pydantic, db from vectordb, and ask from rag. One import per line, in that order.

Create the app

Create a variable called app by calling FastAPI().

Let Angular call the API

Call app.add_middleware() with CORSMiddleware, one argument per line. Set allow_origins to a list holding "http://localhost:4200", and set allow_methods and allow_headers to ["*"].

Describe the /ask body

Write a class Question that extends BaseModel, with one str field: question.

Describe the /add body

Write a class Doc that extends BaseModel, with a str field text and a str field source whose default value is "api".

Add @app.post("/ask"). Below it, define ask_endpoint(body: Question). It returns a dict with the key "answer" and the value ask(body.question).

Write the /add route

Add @app.post("/add") and define add(doc: Doc). Inside it, call db.add_texts() with a list holding doc.text and metadatas=[{"source": doc.source}]. Return {"status": "added"}.

Define the add tool

Create tools as a list holding add and search_docs. Create tools_by_name as a dict comprehension mapping t.name to t for each t in tools.

Create llm_with_tools with llm.bind_tools(tools).

Ask a question that needs a tool

Call llm_with_tools.invoke() with "What is 3 + 4?" into response. Print response.tool_calls.

Run each tool call yourself

Loop over response.tool_calls as call. Inside, look up the tool with tools_by_name[call["name"]] and call its invoke() with call["args"], keeping the result in result. Print call["name"], the text "->", and result.

The order matters, because each step needs the one before it. You will have two or three terminals open.

  2. Open a terminal in the project folder and activate the environment.
  3. Run python chat.py to confirm the key and model work.
  4. Run python ingest.py. The first run downloads the embedding model. Run it again only when notes.txt changes.

Secrets out of the code, one file to swap providers

Interview questions

Try to answer each one aloud before you open it.

Why does the Claude tab use a separate embedding model?

Anthropic doesn't offer an embeddings API. Claude writes the answers, and a different model, here a small open one running locally, turns text into vectors for the search. Any embedding provider works, as long as you use the same one for storing and searching.

What is the difference between ChatAnthropic and ChatOpenAI?

They are LangChain's wrappers for two different APIs. Both give you the same invoke() method and the same message objects, so the rest of your code doesn't change when you swap one for the other.

Why put the model name in .env?

Model names change and old ones are retired. Keeping the name in .env lets you update it without editing code.

Why keep an API key in a .env file?

It keeps secrets out of your source code and out of git. The code only reads an environment variable, so each machine or server can have its own key, and you can change a key without editing any code.

What does load_dotenv() do?

It reads the NAME=value lines of the .env file and adds them to the process's environment variables, so os.getenv can find them. It starts in the folder of the file that calls it and walks up through the parent folders.

Why can't the API key live in the Angular app?

Everything sent to the browser can be read by anyone who opens the developer tools. A key there can be copied and used on your account. The key stays on the backend, and Angular only calls your own endpoints.

Why use a separate Chroma folder after switching embedding models?

Each embedding model makes vectors of its own length, and vectors from different models can't be compared. A collection that already holds one length rejects the other, so use a new folder or re-ingest everything with the new model.

Why does python main.py not start the server?

main.py only creates the app object and its routes. A server such as uvicorn has to load that file and listen for requests, which is why you run uvicorn main:app --reload instead.

The same app, with ChatGPT's models. LangChain talks to OpenAI directly through ChatOpenAI and OpenAIEmbeddings. There is no base_url and no middleman. Your key lives in a .env file read by python-dotenv, and one small file, config.py, builds llm and embeddings for every other file to import.

This tab holds every backend file, from the database to FastAPI. Only quick_add.py, search.py, manage.py and the whole Angular step are identical to the Ollama tab, so copy those over from there. They all do from vectordb import db and work as they are.

On macOS or Linux run source .venv/bin/activate. On Windows run .venv\Scripts\activate. Your prompt then starts with (.venv). Activate it again in every new terminal before you run the project.

The /docs page is good for a first try. A small script is better, because you can run it again after every change.

try_api.py

Create a new, empty try_api.py. It calls your running FastAPI server the same way Angular does: it adds one sentence with /add, then asks about it with /ask.

requests.post() sends an HTTP POST. Passing json= turns the dict into a JSON body and sets the right header, which matches the Doc and Question models in main.py. A status of 200 means it worked. Every run adds the demo sentence again, which is harmless for a test.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Import requests

Import the requests module.

Name the server address

Create API set to "http://localhost:8000".

Add a document

Create added by calling requests.post( with one argument per line: the f-string f"{API}/add", then json= a dict with "text" set to "RBAC stands for Role-Based Access Control." and "source" set to "demo". Close the call with ) on its own line.

Show the result

Print added.status_code and added.json().

Start everything in order

The order matters, because each step needs the one before it. You will have two or three terminals open.

  1. Check that .env sits next to config.py and holds your real key. You don't need Ollama for this tab.
  2. Open a terminal in the project folder and activate the environment.
  3. Run python chat.py to confirm the key and model work.
  4. Run python ingest.py. It embeds your notes through OpenAI, which uses a little credit. Run it again only when notes.txt changes.
  5. Run uvicorn main:app --reload and leave this terminal open.
  6. Open a second terminal in the project folder, activate the environment, and run python try_api.py. You should see 200 and a reply.
  7. Open a third terminal in the frontend folder and run ng serve. Then open http://localhost:4200.

  • Check that .env sits next to config.py and holds your real key.

  • Run python embed.py. The vector length should be 1536.
  • Put a few paragraphs in notes.txt and run python ingest.py. Then run python rag.py.

Secrets out of the code, one file to swap providers

You now have the whole pipeline running on OpenAI, with the key kept in .env and read by config.py. Because every file imports llm and embeddings from one place, moving to Claude or back to Ollama means editing only config.py and its .env.

Interview questions

Try to answer each one aloud before you open it.

What does base_url do, and why isn't it here?

base_url points the OpenAI client at a different server, such as OpenRouter or vLLM. When you call OpenAI itself, you leave it out and the client uses OpenAI's own address.

Why does one OpenAI key cover both chat and embeddings?

Both are products of the same API account, so the same key authorises them. They are billed separately, per model.

Why use a new Chroma folder for this setup?

Each embedding model makes vectors of its own length and meaning. Mixing models in one collection gives meaningless search results or a dimension error, so each setup gets its own folder.

Why keep an API key in a .env file?

It keeps secrets out of your source code and out of git. The code only reads an environment variable, so each machine or server can have its own key, and you can change a key without editing any code.

What does load_dotenv() do?

It reads the NAME=value lines of the .env file and adds them to the process's environment variables, so os.getenv can find them. It starts in the folder of the file that calls it and walks up through the parent folders.

Why can't the API key live in the Angular app?

Everything sent to the browser can be read by anyone who opens the developer tools. A key there can be copied and used on your account. The key stays on the backend, and Angular only calls your own endpoints.

Why use a separate Chroma folder after switching embedding models?

Each embedding model makes vectors of its own length, and vectors from different models can't be compared. A collection that already holds one length rejects the other, so use a new folder or re-ingest everything with the new model.

Why does python main.py not start the server?

main.py only creates the app object and its routes. A server such as uvicorn has to load that file and listen for requests, which is why you run uvicorn main:app --reload instead.

Put your project on GitHub from the command line. You will install Git, tell it who you are, log in to your GitHub account, turn your project folder into a repository, make a commit, and push it. Then you will learn the daily routine, branches, pull requests, and how to fix the usual mistakes. The examples use the rag-app folder from the other tabs, but the steps work for any project.

Use any terminal: Command Prompt (cmd), PowerShell, Terminal on macOS, or a Linux shell. The Git commands are the same everywhere. Where Windows differs, the text says so. Replace YOUR-USERNAME, Your Name and you@example.com with your own details.

Never type a password, token or key into this page. The boxes below save your text in your browser. Practise with the placeholders shown, and type real secrets only in your own terminal.

Step 1 Understand Git and GitHub

Git is a program on your computer. It records snapshots of your project, called commits, so you can see what changed and go back.
GitHub is a website that stores a copy of your repository online, so you can back it up, share it, and work with others. Git is the tool, GitHub is the place you send the snapshots.
Remote: the online copy. By convention it is named origin.

Your files
↓ git add
Staging area (what goes into the next snapshot)
↓ git commit
Local repository (your history)
↓ git push
GitHub (origin)

Step 2 Install Git and say who you are

Install Git from git-scm.com. On Windows, accept the defaults, which also install Git Credential Manager, the helper that remembers your GitHub login. On macOS, run xcode-select --install or use Homebrew. On Ubuntu or Debian, run sudo apt install git. Close and reopen your terminal afterwards.

Check that Git is installed

This prints the version number. If your terminal says the command is not found, Git is not installed yet, or you need to open a new terminal.

Read the commands

Practise them

Check the version

Write the command that prints the Git version.

Set your name and email

Every commit records who made it. --global saves the setting for every project on this computer, so you do this once. Use the same email as your GitHub account, or the private "noreply" address GitHub shows in Settings, Emails. init.defaultBranch main makes new repositories start on a branch called main, which matches what GitHub uses. The last line prints your settings so you can check them.

Read the commands

Practise them

Set name and email

Write two git config --global commands, one per line: user.name set to "Your Name", then user.email set to "you@example.com".

Choose main and check

Add git config --global init.defaultBranch main, then git config --global --list on the next line.

Step 3 Log in to your GitHub account

Create an account at github.com if you don't have one. GitHub no longer accepts your account password for git push. You log in in one of three ways. Option A, the GitHub CLI, is the easiest, so start there.

OptionHow it worksBest for
A. GitHub CLI (gh)You run gh auth login, approve in your browser, and Git is set up to use that login.Most people. Works on every system.
B. Personal access tokenYou create a token on GitHub and paste it when Git asks for a password.When you can't install gh.
C. SSH keyYou make a key pair and give GitHub the public half. No password prompts after that.People who push every day.

Option A: the GitHub CLI

Log in with gh

Install the GitHub CLI from cli.github.com (on Windows you can also run winget install --id GitHub.cli), then open a new terminal. gh auth login asks a few questions. Choose GitHub.com, then HTTPS, answer Yes to "Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials?", and choose Login with a web browser. It shows a one-time code. Press Enter, paste the code on the page that opens, and sign in. gh auth status then confirms who you are logged in as.

Read the commands

Practise them

Log in and check

Write gh auth login, then gh auth status on the next line.

Option B: a personal access token

On GitHub, open your profile picture, then Settings, Developer settings, Personal access tokens, and create a token. A fine-grained token limited to one repository is safest, with read and write access to Contents. A classic token with the repo scope also works. Copy it straight away, because GitHub shows it only once.

The first time you run git push over HTTPS, Git asks for a Username, which is your GitHub username, and a Password, where you paste the token, not your account password. Nothing shows as you paste, which is normal. On Windows, Git Credential Manager remembers it, and it may open a browser sign-in instead, which is also fine. Treat a token like a password: never put it in code, in .env files you commit, or in a chat.

Option C: an SSH key

Make an SSH key and test it

ssh-keygen makes a key pair. Press Enter to accept the default file, and choose a passphrase if you like. The public key is the file ending in .pub. Print it, copy it, and add it on GitHub under Settings, SSH and GPG keys, New SSH key. Never share the file without .pub. The last line checks that GitHub recognises you. On Windows cmd, print the key with type %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub instead of cat.

With SSH, your remote address looks like git@github.com:YOUR-USERNAME/rag-app.git and not https://github.com/.... Use one style consistently.

Read the commands

Practise them

Make and test the key

Write ssh-keygen with -t ed25519 and -C "you@example.com". Then print ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub with cat. Then test with ssh -T git@github.com.

Step 4 Turn your project into a repository

Open your terminal in the project folder. On Windows cmd, change drive and folder in one go with cd /d D:\projects\rag-app (the /d lets cd switch drives). First, tell Git what to leave out.

.gitignore

Create a file named exactly .gitignore in the project folder, before your first commit. Each line is a name or folder Git must never track.

The first line matters most. .env holds your API keys. A key pushed to GitHub can be found and used by anyone, even in a private repository's history if it is ever made public. The other lines skip the virtual environment, the vector databases, Python's cache and the Angular packages, which are large and can be rebuilt.

Read the file

Practise it

Ignore secrets and rebuildable folders

Write nine lines: .env, .venv/, chroma_db/, chroma_db_openrouter/, chroma_db_vllm/, chroma_db_claude/, chroma_db_openai/, __pycache__/ and node_modules/.

Angular makes its own repository. ng new frontend runs git init inside frontend, so Git later treats that folder as a separate repository and skips its files. Before your first git add, delete that hidden folder: rmdir /s /q frontend\.git on Windows cmd, or rm -rf frontend/.git on macOS and Linux. Next time, use ng new frontend --skip-git.

Create the repository

git init creates a hidden .git folder, where Git keeps the history. git status shows what Git sees. Your files appear as "untracked", and .env and .venv should not be listed, because .gitignore hides them.

Run git status between add and commit, and read the green list. If you see .env there, stop: your .gitignore is wrong or misnamed.

Step 6 The daily routine

After the first push, each working session is the same loop: get the latest, change files, review, save a snapshot, and send it.

Pull, change, commit, push

git pull downloads new commits from GitHub, which matters when you work on two computers or with others. After you edit files, git status lists what changed and git diff shows the exact lines. Then you stage, commit with a message that says why, and push.

Look at the history

Step 7 Branches and pull requests

A branch is a separate line of work, so you can try something without touching main. A pull request (PR) asks GitHub to merge your branch into main, and it is where people review the change.

Work on a branch and open a pull request

git switch -c NAME creates a branch and moves onto it. The first push of a new branch needs -u origin NAME. gh pr create --fill opens a pull request using your commit message as the title. You can also click the green button GitHub shows after the push.

Read the commands

Practise them

Create the branch and commit

After the pull request is merged

Merge the pull request on GitHub with the Merge pull request button. Then bring your computer up to date and delete the finished branch. git switch main moves back to main, git pull downloads the merged work, and git branch -d removes the local branch.

Step 9 Fix common mistakes

Stop tracking a file you already committed

Adding a file to .gitignore does not remove it from a repository that already tracks it. git rm --cached removes it from Git but keeps the file on your disk. Use it for .env, or for a folder with -r, such as git rm -r --cached chroma_db.

If a real key was ever pushed, deleting the file is not enough. The old commit still contains it. Treat the key as stolen: delete it in the provider's console, create a new one, and put the new one only in your local .env.

Read the commands

Practise them

Untrack and push

Write git rm --cached .env, then git commit -m "Stop tracking .env", then git push.

Undo cheat sheet

I want toCommandCareful
Throw away my edits to one filegit restore FILEThe edits are gone for good.
Take a file out of staginggit restore --staged FILESafe. The file keeps your edits.
Change the last commit messagegit commit --amend -m "New message"Only before you push it.
Undo a pushed commit safelygit revert HASHAdds a new commit that cancels the old one.
See which commit is whichgit log --onelineThe short id at the start of each line is the HASH.
Avoid git reset --hard and git push --force until you understand them. They can delete work, and a force push can erase other people's commits.

Your project is on GitHub

Install, log in, commit, push

You can now put any folder under version control, connect it to your GitHub account from the command line, and keep it in sync. Good next steps are writing a README.md, protecting the main branch so changes go through pull requests, and adding a GitHub Actions workflow that tests your code on every push.

Interview questions

Try to answer each one aloud before you open it.

What is the difference between Git and GitHub?

Git is the version-control program that runs on your computer and records history. GitHub is a website that hosts copies of Git repositories and adds sharing, pull requests and issues. You can use Git without GitHub.

What do git add, git commit and git push each do?

git add puts changes in the staging area. git commit saves a snapshot of the staged changes in your local history. git push uploads your local commits to the remote repository.

What is origin?

The default name for the remote repository you cloned from or connected with git remote add. It is only a nickname for the address, and you can have several remotes.

What does -u do in git push -u origin main?

It sets the upstream: it links your local main to origin/main, so later git push and git pull know where to go without extra arguments.

Why must .env never be committed?

It holds secrets. Once a commit is pushed, anyone with access can read it, and Git history keeps old versions even after you delete the file. Ignore it with .gitignore, and rotate any key that leaked.

Why does GitHub ask for a token and not my password?

Passwords are weak for command-line use. A token can be limited to certain actions or one repository, can expire, and can be revoked without changing your account password.

HTTPS or SSH, which should I use?

HTTPS works through almost any network and is easy with gh auth login or a token. SSH uses a key pair and never asks for a password after setup. Both reach the same repository.

What is the difference between git pull and git fetch?

git fetch downloads new commits but leaves your files alone. git pull fetches and then merges them into your current branch.

What is a branch, and why open a pull request?

A branch is an independent line of commits, so you can work without disturbing main. A pull request proposes merging it, and gives teammates a place to review and discuss the change first.

What does git clone do that git init does not?

git clone copies an existing repository, with its full history and a remote already set. git init starts a brand-new empty repository with no history and no remote.

PSRS practical: a job recruitment system. You will build a FastAPI back end with MySQL, then a small Angular page. Part 1 is authentication and authorization (registration, login, password reset, roles, sessions, API keys). Part 2 is the recruitment logic (jobs, applications, scoring). Each part is its own module, so you can test it alone before joining them.

Angular page
↓ HTTP + Bearer token
FastAPI: auth.py (Part 1) and recruitment.py (Part 2)
↓ SQLAlchemy
MySQL: users, sessions, password_resets, api_keys, jobs, applications
Never type a real password or key into this page. The boxes save your text in your browser. Use the demo values shown here, and keep real secrets in your own files.

Step 1 Set up the project and the database

On Windows, activate the environment with venv\Scripts\activate. On macOS or Linux, use source venv/bin/activate. Do this each time you open a new terminal.

terminal

Create the folder, install the packages, and create the MySQL database and user.

pymysql talks to MySQL. cryptography is needed for MySQL 8 logins. bcrypt hashes passwords.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Make the project

Write three commands, one per line: make the folder psrs-api, go into it with cd, then create a virtual environment called venv with python -m venv.

Install packages

Write one pip install line for: fastapi uvicorn sqlalchemy pymysql cryptography bcrypt and "pydantic[email]" (in quotes).

Create the database

Run mysql -u root -p -e with one quoted SQL string that creates the database psrs, creates the user psrs@localhost identified by psrs_pass, and grants it all on psrs.*.

Step 2 Database connection and tables

db.py

One place that opens the MySQL connection. Every route asks for a session through get_db.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Engine and session factory

Import create_engine from sqlalchemy, and sessionmaker and DeclarativeBase from sqlalchemy.orm. Create engine for mysql+pymysql://psrs:psrs_pass@localhost/psrs with pool_pre_ping=True, then SessionLocal with sessionmaker(bind=engine, autoflush=False).

Base class

Write class Base(DeclarativeBase): with pass inside.

get_db

Write get_db(): open db = SessionLocal(), yield db inside try, and db.close() in finally.

models.py

Six tables. Tokens and API keys are stored only as SHA-256 hashes, never as the raw value. The unique pair job_id + email stops a candidate applying twice.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Imports

Import datetime from datetime; Boolean, DateTime, ForeignKey, String, Text, UniqueConstraint from sqlalchemy; Mapped, mapped_column from sqlalchemy.orm; and Base from db.

User

Write class User(Base) with __tablename__ = "users", an id primary key, a unique email (String 120), password_hash (String 100) and role (String 20, default "viewer").

Sessions and reset tokens

Write AuthSession (table sessions) and ResetToken (table password_resets). Each has id, a unique token_hash (String 64), user_id (ForeignKey users.id) and expires_at (DateTime). ResetToken also has used, a Boolean defaulting to False.

ApiKey

Write ApiKey (table api_keys) with id, name (String 60), a unique key_hash (String 64) and active (Boolean, default True).

Job

Write Job (table jobs) with id, title (String 120), department (String 80), location (String 80), salary (Mapped[int]) and active (Boolean, default True).

Application

Write Application (table applications) with id, name, email (String 120), job_id (ForeignKey jobs.id), resume (Text), and the integers resume_score, location_points, final_score. Add __table_args__ = (UniqueConstraint("job_id", "email"),).

Step 3 Part 1: authentication and authorization

security.py

The shared helpers: bcrypt hashing, session tokens, the "who is logged in" check, role checks (RBAC) and API key checks. A session token is random, only its hash is saved, and it expires after 2 hours.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Imports

Import hashlib and secrets; datetime, timedelta from datetime; bcrypt; Depends, Header, HTTPException from fastapi; Session from sqlalchemy.orm; get_db from db; and ApiKey, AuthSession, User from models.

Password and hash helpers

Write hash_password(password) using bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt()).decode(), verify_password(password, hashed) using bcrypt.checkpw, and sha(value) returning hashlib.sha256(value.encode()).hexdigest().

Create a session

Write create_session(db, user): make token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32), add an AuthSession with token_hash=sha(token), user_id=user.id and expires_at two hours from datetime.utcnow(), commit, and return the raw token.

Current user

Write current_user(authorization: str = Header(default=""), db: Session = Depends(get_db)). Remove Bearer with removeprefix, find the session by sha(token), and raise HTTPException(401, "Invalid or expired session") if it is missing or expires_at is in the past. Return db.get(User, row.user_id).

Role check (RBAC)

Write require_roles(*roles) that returns an inner function check(user: User = Depends(current_user)). If user.role is not in roles, raise HTTPException(403, "Not allowed for your role"). Otherwise return the user. Return check.

API key check

Write api_key_auth(x_api_key: str = Header(default=""), db: Session = Depends(get_db)). Look up an active ApiKey whose key_hash is sha(x_api_key). If none, raise HTTPException(401, "Invalid API key"). Otherwise return it.

auth.py

The auth routes: register, login, logout, password reset and API key creation. Failed logins are logged. The reset token is printed to the log so you can test; a real system would email it.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Imports and schemas

Import logging, secrets, datetime, timedelta; APIRouter, Depends, Header, HTTPException; BaseModel, EmailStr, Field from pydantic; Session; get_db; the models ApiKey, AuthSession, ResetToken, User; and from security the helpers create_session, current_user, hash_password, require_roles, sha, verify_password. Then make log = logging.getLogger("auth"), router = APIRouter(prefix="/auth", tags=["auth"]), and the schemas Register, Login, Forgot, Reset.

Register

Write POST /register (status 201). If the email already exists, raise HTTPException(409, "Email already registered"). Otherwise save a User with hash_password(body.password), log it, and return the id, email and role.

Login and logout

Write POST /login: if the user is missing or verify_password fails, log a warning and raise HTTPException(401, "Wrong email or password"); otherwise return {"token": create_session(db, user), "role": user.role}. Then POST /logout (needs current_user) that deletes the session with the token from the Authorization header.

Password reset

Write POST /forgot-password: if the user exists, save a ResetToken (hash of a new secrets.token_urlsafe(32), valid 15 minutes) and log the raw token. Always return the same message. Then POST /reset-password: find an unused token, reject it if missing or expired, set the new hashed password, mark it used, delete that user's sessions, commit.

API keys

Write POST /api-keys (status 201, admin only with require_roles("admin")) taking name. Make a raw key with secrets.token_urlsafe(32), save only sha(raw), log who made it, and return the raw key once with a note.

Step 4 Part 2: the recruitment logic

scoring.py

Pure functions with no database, so you can test them alone. The points come from the job location, not the candidate.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Location points

Write location_points(location): make place = location.strip().upper(). Return 3 for "REMOTE", 2 for "DAR ES SALAAM" or "DAR", and 1 for anything else.

Resume and final score

Write resume_score() returning random.randint(1, 10), and final_score(resume, location) returning their sum.

recruitment.py

Jobs and applications. Only admin and editor can add jobs. Anyone can see active jobs. A logged-in user can apply once per job. Third parties read jobs with an API key.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Imports and schemas

Import APIRouter, Depends, HTTPException; BaseModel, EmailStr, Field; Session; get_db; Application, Job, User; final_score, location_points, resume_score from scoring; and api_key_auth, current_user, require_roles from security. Make router = APIRouter(tags=["recruitment"]), the schemas JobIn (title, department, location, salary > 0) and ApplyIn (name, email, job_id, resume), and a helper job_dict(job).

Add and list jobs

Write POST /jobs (status 201, roles admin and editor) that saves Job(**body.model_dump()) and returns its id. Then GET /jobs that returns job_dict for every active job.

Apply

Write POST /applications (status 201, needs current_user). Return 404 if the job is missing or inactive, and 409 "You already applied for this job" if this email already applied. Score it with resume_score(), location_points(job.location) and final_score, save the Application, and return the summary with the message "Application processed successfully.".

Summary and API key route

Write GET /applications/summary (roles admin and editor) that joins Application with Job, sorts by final_score descending, and returns name, position, resume score, location priority and final score. Then GET /external/jobs protected by Depends(api_key_auth) that returns the active jobs.

main.py

The entry point. It creates the tables, allows the Angular page (port 4200) to call the API, and plugs in both routers.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Imports and tables

Import logging, FastAPI, CORSMiddleware from fastapi.middleware.cors, Base, engine from db, and the modules auth and recruitment. Call logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) and Base.metadata.create_all(engine).

App, CORS and routers

Create app = FastAPI(title="PSRS Recruitment"). Add CORSMiddleware allowing origin http://localhost:4200 with all methods and headers. Include auth.router and recruitment.router.

terminal

Start the API. Open http://localhost:8000/docs to try every route.
