Step 6 The Angular page

Needs Node.js and the Angular CLI (npm install -g @angular/cli). The page shows jobs, logs in, and lets a candidate apply.

terminal

Create the Angular app and the jobs component.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Create the app

Write ng new psrs-web --defaults, then cd psrs-web.

Generate and serve

Write ng generate component jobs, then ng serve.

app.config.ts

Replace the whole file in src/app. It turns on HttpClient and attaches the interceptor.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Imports

Import ApplicationConfig from @angular/core, provideHttpClient, withInterceptors from @angular/common/http, and authInterceptor from ./auth.interceptor.

Config

Export appConfig with providers containing provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([authInterceptor])).

auth.interceptor.ts

Create src/app/auth.interceptor.ts. It adds the saved token to every request, so the back end knows who is calling.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Import

Import HttpInterceptorFn from @angular/common/http.

The interceptor

Export authInterceptor as an HttpInterceptorFn with (req, next). Read token from sessionStorage. If there is one, set req to a clone with the header Authorization: Bearer ${token}. Return next(req).

api.service.ts

Create src/app/api.service.ts. Every call to the back end goes through this one class.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Imports

Import HttpClient, Injectable and inject, tap from rxjs. Then set const API = 'http://localhost:8000';.

Class and login

Add @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }) and export class ApiService with private http = inject(HttpClient);. Write login(email, password) that posts to /auth/login and uses tap to save res.token in sessionStorage under 'token'.

Logout

Write logout() that posts to /auth/logout and removes 'token' from sessionStorage with tap.

Jobs and apply

Write jobs() (GET /jobs) and apply(data: object) (POST /applications).

jobs/jobs.ts

Replace src/app/jobs/jobs.ts. A small page: job list, login boxes, and an apply form that shows the score.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Imports

Import Component, inject, OnInit from @angular/core, FormsModule from @angular/forms, and ApiService from ../api.service.

Component and template

Add @Component with selector app-jobs, imports: [FormsModule] and an inline template: a loop over jobs with an Apply button, login inputs and button, name/email/resume inputs, a Submit button, and a {{ message }} line.

Fields

Export class Jobs implements OnInit with private api = inject(ApiService);, jobs: any[] = []; and the string and number fields jobId, name, email, resume, loginEmail, loginPassword, message.

Load and login

Write ngOnInit() that loads the jobs, and login() that calls api.login and sets message to Logged in as ${r.role} or to e.error.detail.

Apply

Write apply() that sends name, email, job_id and resume, then sets message to ${r.position}: final score ${r.final_score} or to e.error.detail.

Last, in src/app/app.ts add Jobs to imports (import { Jobs } from './jobs/jobs';) and put <app-jobs /> in src/app/app.html.

Step 7 Check that it worked

  • Start uvicorn main:app --reload. The terminal should show no errors, and http://localhost:8000/docs should open. In MySQL, USE psrs; SHOW TABLES; lists six tables.
  • Register with POST /auth/register, then in MySQL run UPDATE psrs.users SET role='admin' WHERE email='you@example.com'; to make your first admin. Log in with POST /auth/login and copy the token.
  • Use curl or the Angular page and send Authorization: Bearer <token>. A viewer calling POST /jobs must get 403. An admin gets 201.
  • Add "Software Engineer" in Remote and "HR Officer" in DAR ES SALAAM. GET /jobs lists both. Apply to the first one: the location priority is 3 and the final score equals resume score + 3.
  • Apply to the same job with the same email again. You must get 409.
  • Call POST /auth/logout, then reuse the old token. You must get 401. Call /auth/forgot-password, copy the token from the log, and set a new password with /auth/reset-password.
  • Create a key with POST /auth/api-keys?name=partner as admin, then call GET /external/jobs with the header X-API-Key. Without the header you get 401.

Not included yet

Login, registration and reset pages in Angular (only login is on the jobs page), a "deactivate job" route, rate limiting on login, and automated tests. These are good next steps.

MySQL 8: the ten common DBA interview tasks, from creating tables to reading an execution plan. Each file starts with USE company_db; where needed, so you can run it on its own. Do the steps in order, because later ones use the tables from Step 1.

Practise on a test server only. These commands create and delete things. Never run them on a live database, and never type a real password into this page.

Start here Install MySQL and log in

A database has two parts. The server is the program that stores the data and runs in the background. The client is the tool you type in (a command-line program or a window like Workbench). So you install the server and a client, start the server, and then log in with the client.

1. What to install

SoftwareWhere fromWhat it is for
MySQL Community Server 8.xdev.mysql.com/downloads (on Windows use the MySQL Installer)The server. During setup you choose the password for the root user. Write it down.
MySQL WorkbenchSame site, or inside the MySQL InstallerA window for writing queries and managing users. Optional but friendly.
XAMPP (alternative)apachefriends.orgBundles MariaDB, which uses almost the same commands. Fine for learning, but the interview tasks assume MySQL.

terminal

After the installer finishes, close and reopen your terminal. Then check that the client is found. If your terminal says "not recognized", the program's bin folder is not on your PATH (see the table at the end of this part).

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Check the client

Write mysql --version.

2. Start the server

terminal

The server must be running before you can log in.

Run the net start commands in Command Prompt opened as Administrator. Service names can differ, so open services.msc to see the exact name on your computer. On Linux use sudo systemctl start mysql. On macOS with Homebrew use brew services start mysql.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Start the service

Write net start MySQL80.

3. Log in

terminal

This is the command-line login. You type your password when asked. It stays hidden while you type.

On a fresh Ubuntu server, sudo mysql may log you in as root without a password. Your prompt changes to mysql> when you are in.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Log in as root

Write mysql -u root -p. -u is the user. -p makes it ask for the password.

Log in to another computer

Write the same command with -h 192.168.1.10 (the host) and -P 3306 (the port) before -u root -p.

Prefer a window instead? Open the graphic tool and fill in these boxes:

BoxWhat to enter
Connection nameAnything, for example Local MySQL
Hostname127.0.0.1
Port3306
Usernameroot, then Test Connection and type the password

first_commands.sql

Once you are in, run these to prove the login works and see where you are.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Who am I?

Select VERSION(), then select CURRENT_USER().

List and leave

Write SHOW DATABASES; then EXIT;.

If the login fails

What you seeWhyFix
'mysql' is not recognizedThe MySQL bin folder is not on PATH.Add C:\Program Files\MySQL\MySQL Server 8.0\bin to PATH, or open the "MySQL Command Line Client" from the Start menu.
ERROR 2003 (HY000): Can't connect to MySQL server on 'localhost'The server is not running.Start the service (Step 2).
ERROR 1045 (28000): Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost'Wrong password.Type the password you chose in the installer. If you forgot it, re-run the MySQL Installer and reconfigure the server.

Step 1 Create the database and tables

01_create.sql

Run this in the mysql client as root.

The tables use departments and employees with a department_id link, so the JOIN task works. This replaces the text column department from the task.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Database

Write CREATE DATABASE company_db; then USE company_db;.

departments table

Create departments with id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT and department_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL.

employees table

Create employees with id (same style), name VARCHAR(100), department_id INT, salary DECIMAL(10,2) and a FOREIGN KEY (department_id) REFERENCES departments(id).

Step 2 Insert and query data

02_insert_query.sql

Add rows, then read them back with WHERE and ORDER BY.

  • USE – picks the database the next commands run in.
  • INSERT INTO … VALUES – adds new rows to a table. The brackets after the table name list the columns you fill.
  • SELECT * – reads every column. SELECT name, salary reads only those columns.
  • FROM – names the table to read from.
  • WHERE – keeps only the rows that match a condition, here salary > 500000.
  • ORDER BY – sorts the result. DESC means highest first; ASC (the default) means lowest first.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Insert

Insert IT and Human Resources into departments(department_name) in one statement. Then insert John, department 1, salary 800000 into employees(name, department_id, salary).

Select

Write SELECT * FROM employees;, then select name, salary where salary > 500000 ordered by salary DESC.

Step 3 JOIN

03_join.sql

An INNER JOIN keeps only the rows that match on both sides. Give each table a short alias.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Join

Select e.name and d.department_name from employees e joined to departments d on e.department_id = d.id.

04_view.sql

A view that hides everything except name and salary.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

View

Create employee_view as SELECT name, salary FROM employees, then select everything from it.

Step 5 Users and roles

05_users.sql

Always give the full account name 'user'@'host'. In the task, TO 'analyst' alone would mean 'analyst'@'%', a different account.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

User and grant

Create 'analyst'@'localhost' identified by 'Str0ng_Pass!'. Grant SELECT on company_db.* to it, then show its grants.

Role (MySQL 8)

Create the role report_reader, grant it SELECT on company_db.*, then grant the role to 'analyst'@'localhost'.

Step 6 Backup and restore

terminal

The most common MySQL backup tool is mysqldump. It writes SQL that rebuilds your tables and data. Run these in a normal terminal, not inside the mysql client.

  • -u root – the MySQL username.
  • -p – ask for the password.
  • company_db – the database to back up. Add a table name after it to back up only that table.
  • > – save the output to a file. < feeds a file back in to restore.
  • --all-databases – back up every database, including users and permissions. Useful for DBA work.
  • --single-transaction – takes a consistent copy of InnoDB tables without locking them, so users can keep working.
  • --routines – includes stored procedures and functions.
  • --triggers – includes triggers (on by default, but writing it makes it clear).
To restore one database, it must exist first: run CREATE DATABASE company_db; in mysql if it is missing. For a live database, add the options below. \ at the end of a line means the command continues on the next line (Linux and macOS; in Windows PowerShell use `, or write it all on one line).

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Backup one database

Save company_db to company_db_backup.sql.

Backup all databases

Save every database to all_backup.sql with --all-databases.

Backup one table

Save only the employees table of company_db to employees.sql.

Safe backup of a live database

Back up company_db to company_db_backup.sql with --single-transaction, --routines and --triggers. Put each option on its own line and end every line except the last with \.

Restore one database

Load company_db_backup.sql back into company_db.

Restore all databases

Load all_backup.sql. No database name, because the file creates them.

backup_drill

Interview practical: create data, back it up, delete the database by accident, then restore it. The SQL lines run in the mysql client; the mysqldump and mysql -u root -p lines run in a terminal.

Careful. DROP DATABASE deletes everything in it, including your Step 1–5 tables. If company_db already exists, CREATE DATABASE fails: drop it first or use a test machine.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Create data

Create and use company_db. Make employees with id (auto increment, primary key), name VARCHAR(50) and salary DECIMAL(10,2). Insert John 800000 and Mary 900000 in one statement.

Backup

In the terminal, dump company_db to company_backup.sql.

Accidentally delete

Drop the database.

Restore

Create the empty database again, then load the backup from the terminal.

Check

Use the database and read every row of employees.

Result:

+----+------+-----------+
| id | name | salary    |
+----+------+-----------+
|  1 | John | 800000.00 |
|  2 | Mary | 900000.00 |
+----+------+-----------+

Step 8 Triggers

08_trigger.sql

A BEFORE INSERT trigger changes the new row before it is saved. NEW is the row being inserted.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Trigger

Create before_insert_employee BEFORE INSERT ON employees FOR EACH ROW with SET NEW.salary = IFNULL(NEW.salary, 0);.

Test it

Step 9 RPO, RTO and point-in-time recovery

09_recovery.sql

The binary log records every change. With a full backup plus the binary log you can recover to a moment just before a crash, so the RPO drops from minutes to nearly zero.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Is the binary log on?

Write SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_bin'; then SHOW BINARY LOGS;.

Step 10 Performance troubleshooting

10_performance.sql

Read the plan first. type: ALL in the output means a full table scan.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Read the plan

Write EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM employees WHERE name = 'John';.

Fix it

Create idx_name_salary on employees(name, salary). Then select only name, salary where name = 'John'.

Step 11 More JOINs: LEFT JOIN, three tables, GROUP BY

12_joins.sql

Build on the departments and employees tables. First add a third table, projects.

Human Resources has no employees, so the LEFT JOIN shows it with an empty name. A plain JOIN would hide it.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Add a projects table

Make USE company_db;, then create projects with id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, project_name VARCHAR(80), department_id INT and a foreign key to departments(id). Insert Payroll System (department 1) and Recruitment Drive (department 2) in one statement.

LEFT JOIN

Select d.department_name and e.name from departments d with a LEFT JOIN employees e on e.department_id = d.id. A LEFT JOIN keeps every department, even one with no employee.

Join three tables

Select e.name, d.department_name and p.project_name from employees e. JOIN departments d on e.department_id = d.id, then JOIN projects p on p.department_id = d.id.

JOIN with GROUP BY

Select d.department_name and COUNT(e.id) AS staff from departments d with a LEFT JOIN employees e on e.department_id = d.id, grouped by d.department_name.

Step 12 Views in depth: change, depend, drop

13_views.sql

A view is only a stored query, so it depends on the tables underneath it.

Dependency: MySQL lets you drop a table that a view uses. The view stays but fails with an error when you query it. Check dependencies before you drop anything.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Create a view over a join

Create dept_staff as the department-and-staff-count query (the GROUP BY query from Step 11), then select everything from it.

Change a view

Replace employee_view so it also shows department_id: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW.

What does a view depend on?

Select table_name from information_schema.view_table_usage where view_name = 'employee_view'.

Drop a view

Write DROP VIEW dept_staff;.

Step 13 Roles in depth: revoke, nest, drop

14_roles.sql

Continue with the analyst user and the report_reader role from Step 5.

Role dependency: the user gets the role's rights only while the role is granted and active. Drop the role and the rights go with it.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Take away a direct privilege

Revoke SELECT on company_db.* from 'analyst'@'localhost', then show its grants.

Switch the role on

A role does nothing until it is active. Write SET DEFAULT ROLE report_reader TO 'analyst'@'localhost';, then show grants for the user USING report_reader.

Clean up in order

Revoke the role from the user, drop the role, then drop the user.

Step 14 Triggers in depth: an audit log

15_audit_trigger.sql

Companies keep a record of who changed pay. A trigger can write that record automatically.

OLD is the row before the change and NEW is the row after. A DELETE trigger has only OLD; an INSERT trigger has only NEW.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Audit table

Create salary_audit with id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, employee_id INT, old_salary and new_salary (both DECIMAL(10,2)), and changed_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.

Audit trigger

Create after_update_salary AFTER UPDATE ON employees FOR EACH ROW that inserts OLD.id, OLD.salary, NEW.salary into salary_audit (employee_id, old_salary, new_salary).

Test and remove

Update John's salary to 900000, select everything from salary_audit, then DROP TRIGGER after_update_salary;.

Step 15 RPO and RTO: set a target, choose a backup plan

Two numbers decide your backup plan. RPO is how much data you can lose. RTO is how long you can be down. The business sets them, and you choose the tools to meet them.

TargetWhat it meansWhat you need
RPO 24 hoursYou can lose one day of data.One full backup every night.
RPO 1 hourYou can lose one hour.A nightly full backup plus log backups every hour.
RPO near 0You can lose almost nothing.A standby server that copies every change as it happens.
RTO 4 hoursBack online within 4 hours.Restore from backup, if a test restore proves it fits.
RTO 1 hourBack online within 1 hour.A fast restore (small database, fast disks), or a standby server.
RTO a few minutesAlmost no downtime.Automatic failover to a standby server.
Work it out. Your RTO is 1 hour. The database backup is 60 GB, the restore runs at 30 GB per hour, and checking the data takes 30 minutes. Real recovery time = restore (2 hours) + checking (30 minutes) = 2 hours 30 minutes. You miss the target. The fix is a smaller or faster restore, or a standby server. Rule: RPO = time since the last backup or log. RTO = time to detect + get a server + restore + check.

terminal

Test the restore time (your real RTO) with time, and replay the binary log up to one minute before the crash (point-in-time recovery).

The .sql backup restores the data as of 09:45. The binary log then replays every change from 09:45 to 09:59, so the RPO is one minute, not fifteen. time works on Linux and macOS; in PowerShell use Measure-Command.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Time the restore

Write time in front of the restore command: time mysql -u root -p company_db < backup.sql.

Replay the binary log

Write mysqlbinlog with --start-datetime="2026-10-26 09:45:00" and --stop-datetime="2026-10-26 09:59:00" on the file binlog.000001, then a pipe | into mysql -u root -p.

Step 16 Change data and tables

Interviewers often ask for the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP. You practise on a scratch table, temp_staff, so your real employees table stays safe.

CommandWhat it removesWHERE?Undo?
DELETEThe rows you choose, or all rows, one by one.YesYes, until you commit (see Step 18).
TRUNCATEEvery row at once. The table and its columns stay.NoNo. It commits at once and restarts the AUTO_INCREMENT counter.
DROP TABLEThe whole table: rows, columns and indexes.NoNo. Restore from a backup.

16_change_data.sql

Change rows with UPDATE and DELETE, change the table with ALTER TABLE, then empty it and remove it.

Always write the WHERE. UPDATE or DELETE without it changes every row. Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to see which rows you will touch. TRUNCATE is refused when a foreign key in another table points at the table. A new column holds NULL (or its DEFAULT) in the old rows, and dropping a column deletes its data for good.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Scratch table

Write USE company_db; first. Create temp_staff with id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, name VARCHAR(100) and salary DECIMAL(10,2). Insert Amina 500000, Juma 600000 and Neema 700000 into temp_staff (name, salary) with one statement.

UPDATE

Raise Juma's salary by 10% with salary = salary * 1.10 and a WHERE on the name. Then select everything to see the change.

DELETE

Delete Neema with a WHERE, then select everything again.

ALTER TABLE

Add a column with ALTER TABLE temp_staff ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(20);, then remove it again with ALTER TABLE temp_staff DROP COLUMN phone;.

TRUNCATE and DROP

Empty the table with TRUNCATE TABLE temp_staff;, then remove the table itself with DROP TABLE temp_staff;.

Step 17 Constraints

A constraint is a rule the database enforces for you, so bad data cannot get in.

ConstraintWhat it doesIn this step
PRIMARY KEYIdentifies each row. Unique, never empty, one per table.id
FOREIGN KEYThe value must exist in another table.tasks.department_id
UNIQUENo two rows may share the value.email
NOT NULLThe value is required.name
CHECKThe value must pass a test.age >= 18
DEFAULTThe value used when you give none.status

When you run the three bad inserts, these are the errors to look for:

Rule brokenMessage (the wording may differ a little)
UNIQUEError 1062: Duplicate entry 'amina@example.com' for key ...
NOT NULLError 1364: Field 'name' doesn't have a default value
CHECKError 3819: Check constraint 'contacts_chk_1' is violated

17_constraints.sql

Build a table with UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT, break each rule on purpose, then see ON DELETE CASCADE in action.

Foreign key behaviour. Without ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting a department that still has rows pointing at it is refused. With it, the child rows are deleted too. Use it only where that is what you mean: it can remove a lot of data with one statement. CHECK is enforced from MySQL 8.0.16. MySQL 8 runs in strict mode by default, which is why the missing name is an error.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Table with rules

Write USE company_db; first. Create contacts with id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, age INT CHECK (age >= 18) and status VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'active'.

A good row

Insert Amina (amina@example.com, age 30) giving only the email, name and age. Select everything: the status column was filled in by DEFAULT.

Three bad rows

Write three inserts that each break one rule, and watch each one fail: the same email again (UNIQUE), a row with no name (NOT NULL), and age 15 (CHECK). Use Juma 31, Neema 25 and Baraka 15.

Cascade table

Create tasks with id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, department_id INT, task VARCHAR(100) and a FOREIGN KEY (department_id) REFERENCES departments(id) ON DELETE CASCADE.

Test the cascade

Insert a department called Temp. Insert one task for it with INSERT ... SELECT id, 'Test task' FROM departments WHERE .... Delete the department, then select everything from tasks: the task is gone too.

Clean up

Drop tasks, then contacts.

Step 18 Transactions

A transaction groups statements so they succeed or fail as one unit. The classic example is a bank transfer. ACID is the checklist interviewers expect.

LetterMeaningIn the bank transfer
A: AtomicityAll the changes in the transaction happen, or none do.Amina is never charged without Juma being paid.
C: ConsistencyThe data moves from one valid state to another. Constraints stay true.The total money in the two accounts stays the same.
I: IsolationTransactions running at the same time do not see each other's half-finished work.Another user never sees the money gone from Amina but not yet in Juma.
D: DurabilityAfter COMMIT the data survives a crash.The transfer is still there after a power cut.

Isolation levels say what one transaction may see of another. The table follows the SQL standard; real databases can be stricter.

Isolation levelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantom read
READ UNCOMMITTEDPossiblePossiblePossible
READ COMMITTEDNoPossiblePossible
REPEATABLE READNoNoPossible
SERIALIZABLENoNoNo

18_transactions.sql

Move money between two accounts, undo a mistake with ROLLBACK, undo only part of a transaction with a savepoint, and set an isolation level.

In this database. InnoDB (the normal MySQL engine) runs REPEATABLE READ by default, and autocommit is on: each statement commits alone unless you start a transaction. MyISAM tables have no transactions. Expected balances: after the transfer, Amina 800 and Juma 700. After the rollback they are the same. After the savepoint part, Amina 700 and Juma 800.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Accounts table

Write USE company_db; first. Create accounts with id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, owner VARCHAR(50) and balance DECIMAL(10,2). Insert Amina 1000 and Juma 500 in one statement.

Transfer and COMMIT

Move 200 from Amina to Juma as one transaction: begin with START TRANSACTION;, subtract 200 from Amina, add 200 to Juma, then COMMIT;. Both changes are saved together.

A mistake and ROLLBACK

Begin again and subtract 900 from Amina. Select everything: her balance is now negative. Then ROLLBACK; and select again: the change is gone.

SAVEPOINT

Begin, subtract 100 from Amina, then set a savepoint called after_debit. Add 1000 to Juma by mistake and go back to the savepoint with ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after_debit;. Add the right 100 to Juma and COMMIT;.

Isolation level

Set SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED; for the next transaction, then start one, select everything and commit.

Clean up

Drop accounts.

Step 19 Monitoring and locks

A user phones: "the system is frozen". Usually one session holds a lock and others wait for it. You list the sessions, find who blocks whom, and end the blocker.

ProblemWhat you seeWhat you do
BlockingA query waits: Lock wait timeout exceeded (error 1205)Find the blocker with sys.innodb_lock_waits and kill it, or ask its owner to commit.
DeadlockError 1213: Deadlock found when trying to get lockMySQL rolls one transaction back for you. Run it again.
Idle in a transactionA session did an update and never committed, so others wait on it.Ask the owner to commit or roll back. If you cannot, end the session.

Make a block on purpose (test server only), so you have something to find:

  1. In window 1 run START TRANSACTION; and UPDATE employees SET salary = salary WHERE name = 'John';. Do not commit.
  2. In window 2 run the same UPDATE. It waits. (MySQL gives up after 50 seconds with error 1205, so work quickly.)
  3. In window 3, as root, run the statements below, find window 1's connection and kill it. Window 2 then finishes.

19_monitoring.sql

See who is connected, find the session that blocks the others, and end it.

Before you kill anything: look at what the session is doing and who owns it. A deadlock needs no kill: two sessions each wait for the other, so the database picks one as the victim and rolls it back. To avoid deadlocks, touch rows and tables in the same order everywhere and keep transactions short. You need the PROCESS privilege to see other people's sessions (root has it). Killing a big transaction makes MySQL roll it back, which can take a while.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

List the sessions

Write SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST;, then select id, user, host, db, command, time, state from information_schema.processlist where command <> 'Sleep'.

Find the blocker

Select waiting_pid, waiting_query, blocking_pid, blocking_query, wait_age from the view sys.innodb_lock_waits.

End the blocker

End the blocker with KILL 42;. Use the blocking_pid you found in place of 42.

Read the deadlock report

Write SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS; and look for the section LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK.

Step 20 Stored procedures

20_procedures.sql

A stored procedure is a named block of SQL saved inside the database. You run it with CALL instead of retyping the statements. Needs MySQL 5.0 or later; run it in the mysql client.

  • DELIMITER // – changes the end-of-statement mark, so the ; inside the procedure does not end the CREATE early. DELIMITER ; puts it back.
  • CREATE PROCEDURE name(...) – saves the procedure. IN parameters bring values in; OUT parameters send a value back.
  • BEGIN … END – wraps the statements the procedure runs.
  • SELECT … INTO p_total – puts a query result into a variable or OUT parameter.
  • CALL – runs the procedure. @total is a session variable that catches the OUT value.
  • SHOW PROCEDURE STATUS / DROP PROCEDURE – list the saved procedures / delete one.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

raise_salary

Switch to company_db and set DELIMITER //. Create raise_salary(IN p_dept INT, IN p_pct DECIMAL(5,2)) that multiplies salary by (1 + p_pct / 100) for that department. End it with END //.

count_employees

Create count_employees(IN p_dept INT, OUT p_total INT) that counts the department's employees INTO p_total. End with END //, then DELIMITER ;.

Call them

Give department 1 a 10% raise. Call count_employees for department 1 into @total, then select @total.

List and drop

List the procedures WHERE Db = 'company_db', then drop count_employees.

Step 21 Window functions

21_window_functions.sql

A window function calculates across related rows (a rank, a running total, the row before) and still shows every row. Window functions need MySQL 8.0 or later.

  • OVER (...) – turns a function into a window function: it works across a set of rows but, unlike GROUP BY, keeps every row in the result.
  • ROW_NUMBER() – numbers the rows 1, 2, 3… with no ties.
  • RANK() / DENSE_RANK() – equal values share a rank. RANK then skips numbers (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2).
  • PARTITION BY – restarts the window for each group, here each department.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER – sets the order the window walks through the rows.
  • SUM() / AVG() OVER – a total or average shown next to every row.
  • LAG() / LEAD() – read the value from the row before / after.
  • ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW – the frame: from the first row up to this one, which makes a running total.
Interview favourite: "find the top earner in each department" (last part) and "RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER".

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Add sample rows

Switch to company_db and add Mary (1, 900000), Peter (1, 700000), Asha (2, 600000) and Neema (2, 650000) in one INSERT.

Rank everyone

Select name, department_id, salary with ROW_NUMBER() as row_num, RANK() as rnk and DENSE_RANK() as dense_rnk, all OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC).

Per department

Add PARTITION BY department_id: RANK() by salary as dept_rank, SUM(salary) as dept_total and AVG(salary) as dept_avg.

Previous, next, running total

Ordered by salary: LAG(salary) as prev_salary, LEAD(salary) as next_salary, and a running SUM(salary) with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW as running_total.

Top earner per department

In a subquery ranked, number rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn. Outside, keep rn = 1.

Step 22 Check that it worked

  • Run SHOW TABLES; in company_db. You should see departments, employees and employee_view.
  • Run the JOIN. John shows with IT.
  • Connect as analyst: SELECT works, DELETE FROM employees; must fail with "command denied".
  • Run the dump, drop a row, restore the file, and confirm the row is back.
  • Insert an employee with no salary. The salary is stored as 0.
  • Run the LEFT JOIN. Human Resources appears with an empty name, and the three-table join lists John with IT and Payroll System.
  • Run SHOW TABLES;. The scratch table temp_staff is gone after Step 16.
  • In Step 17 each of the three bad inserts fails with its own error, and SELECT * FROM tasks; returns no rows after the department is deleted.
  • In Step 18 the balances end at Amina 700 and Juma 800, and the 900 subtraction leaves no trace after the rollback.
  • In Step 19 window 2's UPDATE waits until you end window 1's session, then it finishes.
  • Run CALL raise_salary(1, 10); (Oracle and SQL Server: EXEC). The salaries in department 1 go up by 10%.
  • Run the window queries. Every employee still appears, with a rank, the department total next to each row, and one top earner per department in the last query.

Interview questions

What is a view, and why use it?

A view is a saved SELECT that you query like a table. It stores no data of its own. Use it to hide columns (for example salary), to give users a simpler picture of the data, and to reuse a long query.

Why create an index?

An index lets the database find rows without reading the whole table, so searches, joins and sorting on that column are faster. The cost: it uses disk space and makes INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE a little slower.

What are RPO and RTO?

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how long the system may stay down. Example: RPO = 15 minutes, RTO = 1 hour.

The server crashes at 10:00 and backups run every 15 minutes. What is the RPO?

The most you can lose is 15 minutes of data, because the last backup could have been taken at 09:45. To lower the RPO you back up more often or add log-based recovery (see the recovery step).

A query WHERE name='John' is slow. What do you do?

Check the execution plan to see if it scans the whole table. Create an index on name. Select only the columns you need instead of *. Then check the plan again.

What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?

DELETE removes the rows you choose and accepts a WHERE. TRUNCATE empties the whole table quickly and keeps its structure. DROP TABLE removes the table itself. Whether you can undo them depends on the database and on whether you are inside a transaction.

How do you add or remove a column on a table that already has data?

ALTER TABLE with an add or a DROP COLUMN clause. Old rows get NULL or the DEFAULT in a new column. Dropping a column deletes its data, so take a backup first.

What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE?

A table has one primary key, it identifies each row, and it can never be empty. A table can have many UNIQUE constraints, and in most databases a unique column may hold NULL.

What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?

When you delete a parent row, the database deletes the child rows that point at it. Without it, deleting a parent that still has children is refused.

What does ACID mean?

Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: the data stays valid. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work. Durability: committed data survives a crash.

What is the difference between COMMIT and ROLLBACK?

COMMIT makes the changes of the transaction permanent. ROLLBACK undoes them. A savepoint lets you undo only the part after it.

What are the isolation levels?

From weakest to strongest: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE. A stronger level prevents more problems (dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads) but allows less concurrency.

Users say the database is frozen. What do you do?

List the sessions, find the one that blocks the others (SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST or sys.innodb_lock_waits, then KILL the blocking id), check what it is doing and who owns it, and ask the owner to commit. If that is not possible, end the session.

What is a deadlock and how do you avoid it?

Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can move. The database ends one as the victim. Avoid it by accessing tables and rows in the same order and keeping transactions short.

PostgreSQL 14 or newer: the same ten tasks. Run the files in psql. In PostgreSQL you must switch to company_db with \c company_db before Step 2.

Start here Install PostgreSQL and log in

A database has two parts. The server is the program that stores the data and runs in the background. The client is the tool you type in (a command-line program or a window like Workbench). So you install the server and a client, start the server, and then log in with the client.

pgAdmin 4Installed with PostgreSQL (or pgadmin.org)A window for queries and administration.

Step 1 Create the database and tables

01_create.sql

Run this in psql as the postgres user. \c is a psql command that switches database.

The tables use departments and employees with a department_id link, so the JOIN task works. This replaces the text column department from the task. PostgreSQL has no AUTO_INCREMENT: use an identity column (or SERIAL).

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Database

Write CREATE DATABASE company_db; then \c company_db.

departments table

Create departments with id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY and department_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL.

employees table

Create employees with id (same style), name VARCHAR(100), department_id INT REFERENCES departments(id) and salary NUMERIC(10,2).

Step 2 Insert and query data

02_insert_query.sql

Same idea as MySQL. The data type for money is NUMERIC.

  • INSERT INTO … VALUES – adds new rows to a table. The brackets after the table name list the columns you fill.
  • SELECT * – reads every column. SELECT name, salary reads only those columns.
  • FROM – names the table to read from.
  • WHERE – keeps only the rows that match a condition, here salary > 500000.
  • ORDER BY – sorts the result. DESC means highest first; ASC (the default) means lowest first.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Insert

Insert IT and Human Resources into departments(department_name) in one statement. Then insert John, department 1, salary 800000 into employees(name, department_id, salary).

Select

Write SELECT * FROM employees;, then select name, salary where salary > 500000 ordered by salary DESC.

terminal

Function

Add a projects table

13_views.sql

A view is only a stored query, so it depends on the tables underneath it.

Dependency: PostgreSQL refuses DROP TABLE employees; while a view uses it. It says other objects depend on it. DROP TABLE employees CASCADE; would drop the view too, so use CASCADE with care.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Create a view over a join

Create dept_staff as the department-and-staff-count query (the GROUP BY query from Step 11), then select everything from it.

Replace employee_view so it also shows department_id: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW. New columns can only be added at the end.

What does a view depend on?

Drop a view

Write DROP VIEW dept_staff;.

Step 13 Roles in depth: revoke, nest, drop

14_roles.sql

Continue with the analyst user and the report_reader role from Step 5.

Role dependency: PostgreSQL will not drop a role that still holds privileges ("role cannot be dropped because some objects depend on it"). Revoke first, then drop.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Take away a direct privilege

Revoke SELECT on all tables in schema public from analyst. Then select grantee, table_name, privilege_type from information_schema.role_table_grants where grantee IN ('analyst', 'report_reader').

Who is in which role?

Select r.rolname AS role and m.rolname AS member from pg_auth_members a, joined to pg_roles r on r.oid = a.roleid and to pg_roles m on m.oid = a.member.

Clean up in order

Revoke the role from analyst, revoke SELECT on all tables in public from report_reader, drop that role. Then revoke USAGE on schema public and CONNECT on database company_db from analyst, and drop analyst.

Step 14 Triggers in depth: an audit log

15_audit_trigger.sql

Companies keep a record of who changed pay. A trigger can write that record automatically.

UPDATE OF salary fires only when the salary column is changed. In PostgreSQL, DROP TRIGGER must name the table.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Audit table

Create salary_audit with an identity id, employee_id INT, old_salary and new_salary (both NUMERIC(10,2)), and changed_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.

Trigger function

Create log_salary_change() returning trigger as $$. Insert OLD.id, OLD.salary, NEW.salary into salary_audit (employee_id, old_salary, new_salary), then RETURN NEW;. End with $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;.

Trigger

Create after_update_salary AFTER UPDATE OF salary ON employees FOR EACH ROW that runs EXECUTE FUNCTION log_salary_change();.

Test and remove

Update John's salary to 900000, select everything from salary_audit, then DROP TRIGGER after_update_salary ON employees;.

Step 15 RPO and RTO: set a target, choose a backup plan

Two numbers decide your backup plan. RPO is how much data you can lose. RTO is how long you can be down. The business sets them, and you choose the tools to meet them.

TargetWhat it meansWhat you need
RPO 24 hoursYou can lose one day of data.One full backup every night.
RPO 1 hourYou can lose one hour.A nightly full backup plus log backups every hour.
RPO near 0You can lose almost nothing.A standby server that copies every change as it happens.
RTO 4 hoursBack online within 4 hours.Restore from backup, if a test restore proves it fits.
RTO 1 hourBack online within 1 hour.A fast restore (small database, fast disks), or a standby server.
RTO a few minutesAlmost no downtime.Automatic failover to a standby server.
Work it out. Your RTO is 1 hour. The database backup is 60 GB, the restore runs at 30 GB per hour, and checking the data takes 30 minutes. Real recovery time = restore (2 hours) + checking (30 minutes) = 2 hours 30 minutes. You miss the target. The fix is a smaller or faster restore, or a standby server. Rule: RPO = time since the last backup or log. RTO = time to detect + get a server + restore + check.

postgresql.conf

Turn on WAL archiving so every change is copied out. With a base backup plus the archive you can restore to any minute. Edit postgresql.conf and restart the service.

Test the restore time too (your real RTO): time psql -U postgres -d company_db -f backup.sql. Windows paths and copy differ from the Linux cp shown here.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Archive the WAL

Write three settings: wal_level = replica, archive_mode = on, and archive_command = 'cp %p /var/lib/postgresql/archive/%f'.

Recover to a time

When restoring from the base backup, write restore_command = 'cp /var/lib/postgresql/archive/%f %p' and recovery_target_time = '2026-10-26 09:59:00'. Then create an empty file named recovery.signal and start the server.

Step 16 Change data and tables

Interviewers often ask for the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP. You practise on a scratch table, temp_staff, so your real employees table stays safe.

CommandWhat it removesWHERE?Undo?
DELETEThe rows you choose, or all rows, one by one.YesYes, until you commit (see Step 18).
TRUNCATEEvery row at once. The table and its columns stay.NoYes, inside a transaction. Add RESTART IDENTITY to restart the counter.
DROP TABLEThe whole table: rows, columns and indexes.NoYes, inside a transaction you roll back. Otherwise restore from a backup.

16_change_data.sql

Change rows with UPDATE and DELETE, change the table with ALTER TABLE, then empty it and remove it.

Always write the WHERE. UPDATE or DELETE without it changes every row. Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to see which rows you will touch. TRUNCATE is refused when a foreign key in another table points at the table (PostgreSQL needs TRUNCATE ... CASCADE). A new column holds NULL (or its DEFAULT) in the old rows, and dropping a column deletes its data for good.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Scratch table

You are still connected to company_db. Create temp_staff with id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) and salary NUMERIC(10,2). Insert Amina 500000, Juma 600000 and Neema 700000 into temp_staff (name, salary) with one statement.

UPDATE

Raise Juma's salary by 10% with salary = salary * 1.10 and a WHERE on the name. Then select everything to see the change.

DELETE

Delete Neema with a WHERE, then select everything again.

ALTER TABLE

Add a column with ALTER TABLE temp_staff ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(20);, then remove it again with ALTER TABLE temp_staff DROP COLUMN phone;.

TRUNCATE and DROP

Empty the table with TRUNCATE TABLE temp_staff;, then remove the table itself with DROP TABLE temp_staff;.

Step 17 Constraints

A constraint is a rule the database enforces for you, so bad data cannot get in.

ConstraintWhat it doesIn this step
PRIMARY KEYIdentifies each row. Unique, never empty, one per table.id
FOREIGN KEYThe value must exist in another table.tasks.department_id
UNIQUENo two rows may share the value.email
NOT NULLThe value is required.name
CHECKThe value must pass a test.age >= 18
DEFAULTThe value used when you give none.status

When you run the three bad inserts, these are the errors to look for:

Rule brokenMessage (the wording may differ a little)
UNIQUEERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "contacts_email_key"
NOT NULLERROR: null value in column "name" of relation "contacts" violates not-null constraint
CHECKERROR: new row for relation "contacts" violates check constraint "contacts_age_check"

17_constraints.sql

Build a table with UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT, break each rule on purpose, then see ON DELETE CASCADE in action.

Foreign key behaviour. Without ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting a department that still has rows pointing at it is refused. With it, the child rows are deleted too. Use it only where that is what you mean: it can remove a lot of data with one statement.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Table with rules

You are still connected to company_db. Create contacts with id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, age INT CHECK (age >= 18) and status VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'active'.

A good row

Insert Amina (amina@example.com, age 30) giving only the email, name and age. Select everything: the status column was filled in by DEFAULT.

Three bad rows

Write three inserts that each break one rule, and watch each one fail: the same email again (UNIQUE), a row with no name (NOT NULL), and age 15 (CHECK). Use Juma 31, Neema 25 and Baraka 15.

Cascade table

Create tasks with id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, department_id INT REFERENCES departments(id) ON DELETE CASCADE and task VARCHAR(100).

Test the cascade

Insert a department called Temp. Insert one task for it with INSERT ... SELECT id, 'Test task' FROM departments WHERE .... Delete the department, then select everything from tasks: the task is gone too.

Clean up

Drop tasks, then contacts.

Step 18 Transactions

A transaction groups statements so they succeed or fail as one unit. The classic example is a bank transfer. ACID is the checklist interviewers expect.

LetterMeaningIn the bank transfer
A: AtomicityAll the changes in the transaction happen, or none do.Amina is never charged without Juma being paid.
C: ConsistencyThe data moves from one valid state to another. Constraints stay true.The total money in the two accounts stays the same.
I: IsolationTransactions running at the same time do not see each other's half-finished work.Another user never sees the money gone from Amina but not yet in Juma.
D: DurabilityAfter COMMIT the data survives a crash.The transfer is still there after a power cut.

Isolation levels say what one transaction may see of another. The table follows the SQL standard; real databases can be stricter.

Isolation levelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantom read
READ UNCOMMITTEDPossiblePossiblePossible
READ COMMITTEDNoPossiblePossible
REPEATABLE READNoNoPossible
SERIALIZABLENoNoNo

18_transactions.sql

Move money between two accounts, undo a mistake with ROLLBACK, undo only part of a transaction with a savepoint, and set an isolation level.

In this database. PostgreSQL runs READ COMMITTED by default and treats READ UNCOMMITTED like it. Each statement commits alone unless you BEGIN. If a statement fails inside a transaction, the rest is refused until you ROLLBACK. Expected balances: after the transfer, Amina 800 and Juma 700. After the rollback they are the same. After the savepoint part, Amina 700 and Juma 800.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Accounts table

You are still connected to company_db. Create accounts with id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, owner VARCHAR(50) and balance NUMERIC(10,2). Insert Amina 1000 and Juma 500 in one statement.

Transfer and COMMIT

Move 200 from Amina to Juma as one transaction: begin with BEGIN;, subtract 200 from Amina, add 200 to Juma, then COMMIT;. Both changes are saved together.

A mistake and ROLLBACK

Begin again and subtract 900 from Amina. Select everything: her balance is now negative. Then ROLLBACK; and select again: the change is gone.

SAVEPOINT

Begin, subtract 100 from Amina, then set a savepoint called after_debit. Add 1000 to Juma by mistake and go back to the savepoint with ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after_debit;. Add the right 100 to Juma and COMMIT;.

Isolation level

Start a transaction with BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;, select everything and commit.

Clean up

Drop accounts.

Step 19 Monitoring and locks

A user phones: "the system is frozen". Usually one session holds a lock and others wait for it. You list the sessions, find who blocks whom, and end the blocker.

ProblemWhat you seeWhat you do
BlockingA query hangs, and pg_blocking_pids names who holds the lockCancel or terminate the blocker, or ask its owner to commit.
DeadlockError 40P01: deadlock detectedPostgreSQL checks after deadlock_timeout (1 second by default), aborts one transaction and logs the details. Run it again.
Idle in a transactionA session did an update and never committed, so others wait on it.Ask the owner to commit or roll back. If you cannot, end the session.

Make a block on purpose (test server only), so you have something to find:

  1. In window 1 run BEGIN; and UPDATE employees SET salary = salary WHERE name = 'John';. Do not commit.
  2. In window 2 run the same UPDATE. It waits.
  3. In window 3, as postgres, run the statements below, find window 1's pid and end it. Window 2 then finishes.

19_monitoring.sql

See who is connected, find the session that blocks the others, and end it.

Before you kill anything: look at what the session is doing and who owns it. A deadlock needs no kill: two sessions each wait for the other, so the database picks one as the victim and rolls it back. To avoid deadlocks, touch rows and tables in the same order everywhere and keep transactions short. A normal user sees only their own sessions in full. postgres (a superuser) sees everything and can end any session.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

List the sessions

Select pid, usename, state, wait_event_type, query from pg_stat_activity where datname = 'company_db'.

Find the blocker

Select pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by and query from pg_stat_activity where cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0.

End the blocker

Write SELECT pg_cancel_backend(1234);, then SELECT pg_terminate_backend(1234);. Use the blocked_by you found in place of 1234. Cancel stops the running query only; terminate ends the whole connection.

Locks that are waiting

Select locktype, relation::regclass, mode, granted, pid from pg_locks where NOT granted.

Step 20 Stored procedures

20_procedures.sql

A stored procedure is a named block of SQL saved inside the database. In PostgreSQL a PROCEDURE does work and is run with CALL; a FUNCTION returns a value and is used inside SELECT. Procedures need PostgreSQL 11 or later.

  • CREATE PROCEDURE name(...) – saves the procedure with its parameters.
  • LANGUAGE plpgsql – the procedural language that allows BEGIN … END, variables and IF. LANGUAGE sql is for a plain query.
  • AS $$ … $$ – dollar quotes hold the body, so you do not have to escape quotes inside it.
  • CREATE FUNCTION … RETURNS INT – a function that gives back one value.
  • CALL / SELECT fn() – run a procedure / use a function.
  • pg_proc / DROP FUNCTION – the catalog of procedures and functions (prokind is p or f) / delete one.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

raise_salary

Create raise_salary(p_dept INT, p_pct NUMERIC) in LANGUAGE plpgsql. Between $$ marks, BEGIN an UPDATE that multiplies salary by (1 + p_pct / 100) for that department, then END;.

count_employees

Create the function count_employees(p_dept INT) RETURNS INT in LANGUAGE sql that returns COUNT(*)::INT for the department.

Call them

Give department 1 a 10% raise with CALL, then select count_employees(1).

List and drop

Select proname, prokind from pg_proc for the two names, then drop the function.

Step 21 Window functions

21_window_functions.sql

A window function calculates across related rows (a rank, a running total, the row before) and still shows every row.

  • OVER (...) – turns a function into a window function: it works across a set of rows but, unlike GROUP BY, keeps every row in the result.
  • ROW_NUMBER() – numbers the rows 1, 2, 3… with no ties.
  • RANK() / DENSE_RANK() – equal values share a rank. RANK then skips numbers (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2).
  • PARTITION BY – restarts the window for each group, here each department.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER – sets the order the window walks through the rows.
  • SUM() / AVG() OVER – a total or average shown next to every row.
  • LAG() / LEAD() – read the value from the row before / after.
  • ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW – the frame: from the first row up to this one, which makes a running total.
Interview favourite: "find the top earner in each department" (last part) and "RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER".

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Add sample rows

Add Mary (1, 900000), Peter (1, 700000), Asha (2, 600000) and Neema (2, 650000) in one INSERT.

Rank everyone

Select name, department_id, salary with ROW_NUMBER() as row_num, RANK() as rnk and DENSE_RANK() as dense_rnk, all OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC).

Per department

Add PARTITION BY department_id: RANK() by salary as dept_rank, SUM(salary) as dept_total and AVG(salary) as dept_avg.

Previous, next, running total

Ordered by salary: LAG(salary) as prev_salary, LEAD(salary) as next_salary, and a running SUM(salary) with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW as running_total.

Top earner per department

In a subquery ranked, number rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn. Outside, keep rn = 1.

  • In psql run \dt. You should see departments and employees, and \dv shows employee_view.
  • Run the JOIN. John shows with IT.
  • Connect as analyst with psql -U analyst -d company_db: SELECT works, DELETE FROM employees; fails with "permission denied".
  • Back up, delete a row, restore, and confirm the row is back.
  • Insert an employee with no salary. The trigger stores 0.
  • Run the LEFT JOIN. Human Resources appears with an empty name, and the three-table join lists John with IT and Payroll System.
  • Run \dt. The scratch table temp_staff is gone after Step 16.
  • In Step 17 each of the three bad inserts fails with its own error, and SELECT * FROM tasks; returns no rows after the department is deleted.
  • In Step 18 the balances end at Amina 700 and Juma 800, and the 900 subtraction leaves no trace after the rollback.
  • In Step 19 window 2's UPDATE waits until you end window 1's session, then it finishes.
  • Run CALL raise_salary(1, 10); (Oracle and SQL Server: EXEC). The salaries in department 1 go up by 10%.
  • Run the window queries. Every employee still appears, with a rank, the department total next to each row, and one top earner per department in the last query.

Interview questions

What is a view, and why use it?

A view is a saved SELECT that you query like a table. It stores no data of its own. Use it to hide columns (for example salary), to give users a simpler picture of the data, and to reuse a long query.

Why create an index?

An index lets the database find rows without reading the whole table, so searches, joins and sorting on that column are faster. The cost: it uses disk space and makes INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE a little slower.

What are RPO and RTO?

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how long the system may stay down. Example: RPO = 15 minutes, RTO = 1 hour.

The server crashes at 10:00 and backups run every 15 minutes. What is the RPO?

The most you can lose is 15 minutes of data, because the last backup could have been taken at 09:45. To lower the RPO you back up more often or add log-based recovery (see the recovery step).

A query WHERE name='John' is slow. What do you do?

Check the execution plan to see if it scans the whole table. Create an index on name. Select only the columns you need instead of *. Then check the plan again.

What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?

DELETE removes the rows you choose and accepts a WHERE. TRUNCATE empties the whole table quickly and keeps its structure. DROP TABLE removes the table itself. Whether you can undo them depends on the database and on whether you are inside a transaction.

How do you add or remove a column on a table that already has data?

ALTER TABLE with an add or a DROP COLUMN clause. Old rows get NULL or the DEFAULT in a new column. Dropping a column deletes its data, so take a backup first.

What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE?

A table has one primary key, it identifies each row, and it can never be empty. A table can have many UNIQUE constraints, and in most databases a unique column may hold NULL.

What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?

When you delete a parent row, the database deletes the child rows that point at it. Without it, deleting a parent that still has children is refused.

What does ACID mean?

Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: the data stays valid. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work. Durability: committed data survives a crash.

What is the difference between COMMIT and ROLLBACK?

COMMIT makes the changes of the transaction permanent. ROLLBACK undoes them. A savepoint lets you undo only the part after it.

What are the isolation levels?

From weakest to strongest: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE. A stronger level prevents more problems (dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads) but allows less concurrency.

Users say the database is frozen. What do you do?

List the sessions, find the one that blocks the others (pg_stat_activity and pg_blocking_pids, then pg_terminate_backend), check what it is doing and who owns it, and ask the owner to commit. If that is not possible, end the session.

What is a deadlock and how do you avoid it?

Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can move. The database ends one as the victim. Avoid it by accessing tables and rows in the same order and keeping transactions short.

Oracle Database 12c or newer (Oracle XE is free). Use SQL*Plus or SQL Developer. Step 1 creates the schema and Step 5 needs a DBA account. Oracle differs from the other three in several small ways, and the notes point them out.

Practise on a test server only. These commands create and delete things. Never run them on a live database, and never type a real password into this page.

Start here Install Oracle and log in

A database has two parts. The server is the program that stores the data and runs in the background. The client is the tool you type in (a command-line program or a window like Workbench). So you install the server and a client, start the server, and then log in with the client. In Oracle, a "database" is also called an instance, and users own schemas.

1. What to install

SoftwareWhere fromWhat it is for
Oracle Database Free or Express Edition (XE) 21coracle.com/database (free download)The server. The installer asks for one password, used for SYS and SYSTEM. Note: XE names its pluggable database XEPDB1, Free names it FREEPDB1.
SQL*PlusInstalled with the databaseThe command-line client.
Oracle SQL Developeroracle.com/database/sqldeveloperA window for queries and administration.

terminal

After the installer finishes, close and reopen your terminal. Then check that the client is found. If your terminal says "not recognized", the program's bin folder is not on your PATH (see the table at the end of this part).

Run the net start commands in Command Prompt opened as Administrator. Service names can differ, so open services.msc to see the exact name on your computer. On Linux, start the database with the service script the installer created (for XE 21c: sudo /etc/init.d/oracle-xe-21c start).

What you seeWhyFix

Step 1 Create the schema and tables

01_create.sql

In Oracle a schema is a user, so "create the database" means creating the user company_db as a DBA. Connect to a pluggable database such as XEPDB1 (Oracle XE) first. In a container database, Oracle may require common user names to start with C##; a pluggable database does not.

The tables use departments and employees with a department_id link, so the JOIN task works. This replaces the text column department from the task. Oracle uses VARCHAR2 and NUMBER. Identity columns need Oracle 12c or newer.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Create the schema user

As DBA, create the user company_db identified by "Str0ng_Pass1" with QUOTA UNLIMITED ON users. Grant it CREATE SESSION, CREATE TABLE, CREATE VIEW, CREATE TRIGGER.

Connect

Write CONNECT company_db/Str0ng_Pass1@localhost/XEPDB1.

departments table

Create departments with id NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY and department_name VARCHAR2(50) NOT NULL.

employees table

Create employees with id (same style), name VARCHAR2(100), department_id NUMBER REFERENCES departments(id) and salary NUMBER(10,2).

Step 2 Insert and query data

02_insert_query.sql

Oracle does not accept a list of rows in one VALUES, so use one INSERT per row. Oracle does not save changes until you COMMIT.

  • INSERT INTO … VALUES – adds new rows to a table. The brackets after the table name list the columns you fill.
  • COMMIT – saves your inserts for good. Without it, other sessions cannot see the new rows.
  • SELECT * – reads every column. SELECT name, salary reads only those columns.
  • FROM – names the table to read from.
  • WHERE – keeps only the rows that match a condition, here salary > 500000.
  • ORDER BY – sorts the result. DESC means highest first; ASC (the default) means lowest first.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Insert

Insert 'IT' and then 'Human Resources' into departments (department_name) with two statements. Insert 'John', 1, 800000 into employees (name, department_id, salary). Finish with COMMIT;.

Select

Write SELECT * FROM employees;, then select name, salary where salary > 500000 ordered by salary DESC.

Step 14 Triggers in depth: an audit log

15_audit_trigger.sql

Companies keep a record of who changed pay. A trigger can write that record automatically.

:OLD is the row before the change and :NEW is the row after. A trigger runs inside your transaction, so the audit row is saved or rolled back together with the update.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Audit table

Create salary_audit with an identity id, employee_id NUMBER, old_salary and new_salary (both NUMBER(10,2)), and changed_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT SYSTIMESTAMP.

Audit trigger

Create or replace after_update_salary AFTER UPDATE OF salary ON employees FOR EACH ROW. In BEGIN ... END; insert :OLD.id, :OLD.salary, :NEW.salary into salary_audit (employee_id, old_salary, new_salary). Finish with /.

Test and remove

Update John's salary to 900000, COMMIT;, select everything from salary_audit, then DROP TRIGGER after_update_salary;.

Step 15 RPO and RTO: set a target, choose a backup plan

Two numbers decide your backup plan. RPO is how much data you can lose. RTO is how long you can be down. The business sets them, and you choose the tools to meet them.

TargetWhat it meansWhat you need
RPO 24 hoursYou can lose one day of data.One full backup every night.
RPO 1 hourYou can lose one hour.A nightly full backup plus log backups every hour.
RPO near 0You can lose almost nothing.A standby server that copies every change as it happens.
RTO 4 hoursBack online within 4 hours.Restore from backup, if a test restore proves it fits.
RTO 1 hourBack online within 1 hour.A fast restore (small database, fast disks), or a standby server.
RTO a few minutesAlmost no downtime.Automatic failover to a standby server.
Work it out. Your RTO is 1 hour. The database backup is 60 GB, the restore runs at 30 GB per hour, and checking the data takes 30 minutes. Real recovery time = restore (2 hours) + checking (30 minutes) = 2 hours 30 minutes. You miss the target. The fix is a smaller or faster restore, or a standby server. Rule: RPO = time since the last backup or log. RTO = time to detect + get a server + restore + check.

recovery.sql

Point-in-time recovery needs archive log mode, so Oracle keeps every redo log. Run this as SYSDBA. It restarts the database, so do it on a test server.

Then recover with RMAN. In an rman target / session, with the database mounted, run RUN { SET UNTIL TIME "TO_DATE('2026-10-26 09:59:00','YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS')"; RESTORE DATABASE; RECOVER DATABASE; } and finish with ALTER DATABASE OPEN RESETLOGS;. Time the RESTORE step: that is your real RTO.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Turn on archive log mode

Write SHUTDOWN IMMEDIATE;, STARTUP MOUNT;, ALTER DATABASE ARCHIVELOG; and ALTER DATABASE OPEN;, one per line.

Step 16 Change data and tables

Interviewers often ask for the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP. You practise on a scratch table, temp_staff, so your real employees table stays safe.

CommandWhat it removesWHERE?Undo?
DELETEThe rows you choose, or all rows, one by one.YesYes, until you commit (see Step 18).
TRUNCATEEvery row at once. The table and its columns stay.NoNo. It commits at once.
DROP TABLEThe whole table: rows, columns and indexes.NoUsually yes: the table goes to the recycle bin and FLASHBACK TABLE ... TO BEFORE DROP brings it back. DROP TABLE ... PURGE skips the bin.

16_change_data.sql

Change rows with UPDATE and DELETE, change the table with ALTER TABLE, then empty it and remove it.

Always write the WHERE. UPDATE or DELETE without it changes every row. Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to see which rows you will touch. TRUNCATE is refused when a foreign key in another table points at the table. A new column holds NULL (or its DEFAULT) in the old rows, and dropping a column deletes its data for good.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Scratch table

You are still connected as company_db. Create temp_staff with id NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR2(100) and salary NUMBER(10,2). Insert Amina 500000, Juma 600000 and Neema 700000 into temp_staff (name, salary) with three statements, then COMMIT;.

UPDATE

Raise Juma's salary by 10% with salary = salary * 1.10 and a WHERE on the name. Then select everything to see the change.

DELETE

Delete Neema with a WHERE, then select everything again. Finish with COMMIT;.

ALTER TABLE

Add a column with ALTER TABLE temp_staff ADD (phone VARCHAR2(20));, then remove it again with ALTER TABLE temp_staff DROP COLUMN phone;.

TRUNCATE and DROP

Empty the table with TRUNCATE TABLE temp_staff;, then remove the table itself with DROP TABLE temp_staff;.

Step 17 Constraints

A constraint is a rule the database enforces for you, so bad data cannot get in.

ConstraintWhat it doesIn this step
PRIMARY KEYIdentifies each row. Unique, never empty, one per table.id
FOREIGN KEYThe value must exist in another table.tasks.department_id
UNIQUENo two rows may share the value.email
NOT NULLThe value is required.name
CHECKThe value must pass a test.age >= 18
DEFAULTThe value used when you give none.status

When you run the three bad inserts, these are the errors to look for:

Rule brokenMessage (the wording may differ a little)
UNIQUEORA-00001: unique constraint (COMPANY_DB.SYS_C...) violated
NOT NULLORA-01400: cannot insert NULL into ("COMPANY_DB"."CONTACTS"."NAME")
CHECKORA-02290: check constraint (COMPANY_DB.SYS_C...) violated

17_constraints.sql

Build a table with UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT, break each rule on purpose, then see ON DELETE CASCADE in action.

Foreign key behaviour. Without ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting a department that still has rows pointing at it is refused. With it, the child rows are deleted too. Use it only where that is what you mean: it can remove a lot of data with one statement.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Table with rules

You are still connected as company_db. Create contacts with id NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR2(100) UNIQUE, name VARCHAR2(100) NOT NULL, age NUMBER CHECK (age >= 18) and status VARCHAR2(10) DEFAULT 'active'.

A good row

Insert Amina (amina@example.com, age 30) giving only the email, name and age. Then COMMIT;. Select everything: the status column was filled in by DEFAULT.

Three bad rows

Write three inserts that each break one rule, and watch each one fail: the same email again (UNIQUE), a row with no name (NOT NULL), and age 15 (CHECK). Use Juma 31, Neema 25 and Baraka 15.

Cascade table

Create tasks with id NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, department_id NUMBER REFERENCES departments(id) ON DELETE CASCADE and task VARCHAR2(100).

Test the cascade

Insert a department called Temp. Insert one task for it with INSERT ... SELECT id, 'Test task' FROM departments WHERE .... Delete the department, then select everything from tasks: the task is gone too. Finish with COMMIT;.

Clean up

Drop tasks, then contacts.

Step 18 Transactions

A transaction groups statements so they succeed or fail as one unit. The classic example is a bank transfer. ACID is the checklist interviewers expect.

LetterMeaningIn the bank transfer
A: AtomicityAll the changes in the transaction happen, or none do.Amina is never charged without Juma being paid.
C: ConsistencyThe data moves from one valid state to another. Constraints stay true.The total money in the two accounts stays the same.
I: IsolationTransactions running at the same time do not see each other's half-finished work.Another user never sees the money gone from Amina but not yet in Juma.
D: DurabilityAfter COMMIT the data survives a crash.The transfer is still there after a power cut.

Isolation levels say what one transaction may see of another. The table follows the SQL standard; real databases can be stricter.

Isolation levelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantom read
READ UNCOMMITTEDPossiblePossiblePossible
READ COMMITTEDNoPossiblePossible
REPEATABLE READNoNoPossible
SERIALIZABLENoNoNo

18_transactions.sql

Move money between two accounts, undo a mistake with ROLLBACK, undo only part of a transaction with a savepoint, and set an isolation level.

In this database. Oracle runs READ COMMITTED by default and offers only that, SERIALIZABLE and READ ONLY. It never allows dirty reads. A transaction ends with COMMIT or ROLLBACK, and DDL such as CREATE TABLE commits by itself. Expected balances: after the transfer, Amina 800 and Juma 700. After the rollback they are the same. After the savepoint part, Amina 700 and Juma 800.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Accounts table

You are still connected as company_db. Create accounts with id NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, owner VARCHAR2(50) and balance NUMBER(10,2). Insert Amina 1000 and Juma 500 with two statements, then COMMIT;.

Transfer and COMMIT

Move 200 from Amina to Juma as one transaction: begin with nothing: Oracle starts a transaction by itself at your first change, subtract 200 from Amina, add 200 to Juma, then COMMIT;. Both changes are saved together.

A mistake and ROLLBACK

Begin again and subtract 900 from Amina. Select everything: her balance is now negative. Then ROLLBACK; and select again: the change is gone.

SAVEPOINT

Begin, subtract 100 from Amina, then set a savepoint called after_debit. Add 1000 to Juma by mistake and go back to the savepoint with ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after_debit;. Add the right 100 to Juma and COMMIT;.

Isolation level

Write SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; (it must be the first statement of a transaction, which is why the last COMMIT came just before), select everything and commit.

Clean up

Drop accounts.

Step 19 Monitoring and locks

A user phones: "the system is frozen". Usually one session holds a lock and others wait for it. You list the sessions, find who blocks whom, and end the blocker.

ProblemWhat you seeWhat you do
BlockingA statement waits, and v$session.blocking_session names the blockerKill the blocker, or ask its owner to commit or roll back.
DeadlockORA-00060: deadlock detected while waiting for resourceOracle rolls back one statement and writes a trace file. Run the work again and look at the trace to see which rows clashed.
Idle in a transactionA session did an update and never committed, so others wait on it.Ask the owner to commit or roll back. If you cannot, end the session.

Make a block on purpose (test server only), so you have something to find:

  1. In window 1, as company_db, run UPDATE employees SET salary = salary WHERE name = 'John';. Do not commit.
  2. In window 2, as company_db, run the same UPDATE. It waits.
  3. In window 3, connected to the pluggable database as a DBA, run the statements below, find window 1's sid and serial# and kill it. Window 2 then finishes.

19_monitoring.sql

See who is connected, find the session that blocks the others, and end it.

Before you kill anything: look at what the session is doing and who owns it. A deadlock needs no kill: two sessions each wait for the other, so the database picks one as the victim and rolls it back. To avoid deadlocks, touch rows and tables in the same order everywhere and keep transactions short. The v$ views and ALTER SYSTEM need DBA rights, so run this file as a DBA, not as company_db. The killed session shows as KILLED until Oracle finishes rolling it back.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

List the sessions

Select sid, serial#, username, status, osuser, machine from v$session where username IS NOT NULL.

Find the blocker

Select sid, serial#, username, blocking_session, wait_class, seconds_in_wait from v$session where blocking_session IS NOT NULL. The blocking_session column holds the sid of the blocker.

End the blocker

Write ALTER SYSTEM KILL SESSION '123,4567' IMMEDIATE;. The two numbers are the blocker's sid and serial#, which you read from v$session.

Locks that wait or block

Select sid, type, lmode, request, block from v$lock where request > 0 OR block = 1.

Step 20 Stored procedures

20_procedures.sql

A stored procedure is a named PL/SQL block saved inside the database. You run it with EXEC instead of retyping the statements. Run this as company_db in SQL*Plus or SQLcl.

  • CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE – saves the procedure, replacing an older version with the same name.
  • p_dept IN NUMBER / p_total OUT NUMBER – parameters: IN brings a value in, OUT sends one back.
  • AS BEGIN … END; – the PL/SQL body. / on its own line runs the block.
  • SELECT … INTO – puts a query result into a variable.
  • VARIABLE / EXEC / PRINT – make a SQL*Plus variable, run the procedure, show the value.
  • user_objects / DROP PROCEDURE – list your procedures and whether they are VALID / delete one.
Your company_db user needs the right to create procedures. As a DBA run GRANT CREATE PROCEDURE TO company_db; once.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

raise_salary

Create or replace raise_salary(p_dept IN NUMBER, p_pct IN NUMBER). Its body updates salary to salary * (1 + p_pct / 100) for that department, then COMMIT;. Finish with /.

count_employees

Create or replace count_employees(p_dept IN NUMBER, p_total OUT NUMBER) that counts the department's employees INTO p_total. Finish with /.

Call them

Run raise_salary(1, 10). Declare VARIABLE total NUMBER, run count_employees(1, :total) and PRINT total.

List and drop

Select object_name, status from user_objects where object_type = 'PROCEDURE', then drop count_employees.

Step 21 Window functions

21_window_functions.sql

A window function calculates across related rows (a rank, a running total, the row before) and still shows every row.

  • OVER (...) – turns a function into a window function: it works across a set of rows but, unlike GROUP BY, keeps every row in the result.
  • ROW_NUMBER() – numbers the rows 1, 2, 3… with no ties.
  • RANK() / DENSE_RANK() – equal values share a rank. RANK then skips numbers (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2).
  • PARTITION BY – restarts the window for each group, here each department.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER – sets the order the window walks through the rows.
  • SUM() / AVG() OVER – a total or average shown next to every row.
  • LAG() / LEAD() – read the value from the row before / after.
  • ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW – the frame: from the first row up to this one, which makes a running total.
Interview favourite: "find the top earner in each department" (last part) and "RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER".

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Add sample rows

Add Mary (1, 900000), Peter (1, 700000), Asha (2, 600000) and Neema (2, 650000) with one INSERT each, then COMMIT;.

Rank everyone

Select name, department_id, salary with ROW_NUMBER() as row_num, RANK() as rnk and DENSE_RANK() as dense_rnk, all OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC).

Per department

Add PARTITION BY department_id: RANK() by salary as dept_rank, SUM(salary) as dept_total and AVG(salary) as dept_avg.

Previous, next, running total

Ordered by salary: LAG(salary) as prev_salary, LEAD(salary) as next_salary, and a running SUM(salary) with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW as running_total.

Top earner per department

In a subquery ranked, number rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn. Outside, keep rn = 1.
