  • As company_db run SELECT table_name FROM user_tables;. You should see DEPARTMENTS and EMPLOYEES.
  • Run the JOIN. John shows with IT.
  • Connect as analyst: SELECT * FROM company_db.employees; works, DELETE FROM company_db.employees; fails with ORA-01031 (insufficient privileges).
  • Run expdp, check that company_db.dmp exists in the DATA_PUMP_DIR folder, then run impdp.
  • Insert an employee with no salary. The trigger stores 0.
  • Run the LEFT JOIN. Human Resources appears with an empty name, and the three-table join lists John with IT and Payroll System.
  • Run SELECT table_name FROM user_tables;. The scratch table temp_staff is gone after Step 16.
  • In Step 17 each of the three bad inserts fails with its own error, and SELECT * FROM tasks; returns no rows after the department is deleted.
  • In Step 18 the balances end at Amina 700 and Juma 800, and the 900 subtraction leaves no trace after the rollback.
  • In Step 19 window 2's UPDATE waits until you end window 1's session, then it finishes.
  • Run CALL raise_salary(1, 10); (Oracle and SQL Server: EXEC). The salaries in department 1 go up by 10%.
  • Run the window queries. Every employee still appears, with a rank, the department total next to each row, and one top earner per department in the last query.

Interview questions

What is a view, and why use it?

A view is a saved SELECT that you query like a table. It stores no data of its own. Use it to hide columns (for example salary), to give users a simpler picture of the data, and to reuse a long query.

Why create an index?

An index lets the database find rows without reading the whole table, so searches, joins and sorting on that column are faster. The cost: it uses disk space and makes INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE a little slower.

What are RPO and RTO?

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how long the system may stay down. Example: RPO = 15 minutes, RTO = 1 hour.

The server crashes at 10:00 and backups run every 15 minutes. What is the RPO?

The most you can lose is 15 minutes of data, because the last backup could have been taken at 09:45. To lower the RPO you back up more often or add log-based recovery (see the recovery step).

A query WHERE name='John' is slow. What do you do?

Check the execution plan to see if it scans the whole table. Create an index on name. Select only the columns you need instead of *. Then check the plan again.

What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?

DELETE removes the rows you choose and accepts a WHERE. TRUNCATE empties the whole table quickly and keeps its structure. DROP TABLE removes the table itself. Whether you can undo them depends on the database and on whether you are inside a transaction.

How do you add or remove a column on a table that already has data?

ALTER TABLE with an add or a DROP COLUMN clause. Old rows get NULL or the DEFAULT in a new column. Dropping a column deletes its data, so take a backup first.

What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE?

A table has one primary key, it identifies each row, and it can never be empty. A table can have many UNIQUE constraints, and in most databases a unique column may hold NULL.

What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?

When you delete a parent row, the database deletes the child rows that point at it. Without it, deleting a parent that still has children is refused.

What does ACID mean?

Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: the data stays valid. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work. Durability: committed data survives a crash.

What is the difference between COMMIT and ROLLBACK?

COMMIT makes the changes of the transaction permanent. ROLLBACK undoes them. A savepoint lets you undo only the part after it.

What are the isolation levels?

From weakest to strongest: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE. A stronger level prevents more problems (dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads) but allows less concurrency.

Users say the database is frozen. What do you do?

List the sessions, find the one that blocks the others (v$session (the blocking_session column), then ALTER SYSTEM KILL SESSION), check what it is doing and who owns it, and ask the owner to commit. If that is not possible, end the session.

What is a deadlock and how do you avoid it?

Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can move. The database ends one as the victim. Avoid it by accessing tables and rows in the same order and keeping transactions short.

SQL Server 2019 or newer (the free Developer or Express edition works). Use SSMS or sqlcmd. Remember: GO ends a batch, and a few statements (CREATE VIEW, CREATE TRIGGER) must be the first in their batch.

Practise on a test server only. These commands create and delete things. Never run them on a live database, and never type a real password into this page.

Start here Install SQL Server and log in

A database has two parts. The server is the program that stores the data and runs in the background. The client is the tool you type in (a command-line program or a window like Workbench). So you install the server and a client, start the server, and then log in with the client.

1. What to install

SoftwareWhere fromWhat it is for
SQL Server 2022 (Developer or Express edition)microsoft.com/sql-server/sql-server-downloadsThe server. In setup choose "Mixed Mode" and set a password for the sa account. Windows login also works.
SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)Search "SSMS download" on microsoft.com (separate installer)The window for queries and administration.
sqlcmdInstalled with the server toolsThe command-line client.

terminal

After the installer finishes, close and reopen your terminal. Then check that the client is found. If your terminal says "not recognized", the program's bin folder is not on your PATH (see the table at the end of this part).

If the login fails

What you seeWhyFix
Login failed for user 'sa'The password is wrong, or SQL logins are off because you chose Windows-only mode.Use -E instead, or switch the server to Mixed Mode in SSMS (server Properties, Security) and restart the service.

Step 1 Create the database and tables

01_create.sql

Run this in SSMS or sqlcmd. GO is not SQL: it is a tool command that ends a batch and sends it to the server.

The tables use departments and employees with a department_id link, so the JOIN task works. This replaces the text column department from the task. SQL Server uses IDENTITY(1,1) instead of AUTO_INCREMENT.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Database

Write CREATE DATABASE company_db; GO USE company_db; GO, each on its own line.

departments table

Create departments with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY and department_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL.

employees table

Create employees with id (same style), name VARCHAR(100), department_id INT FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES departments(id) and salary DECIMAL(10,2). End with GO.

Step 2 Insert and query data

02_insert_query.sql

Add rows, then read them back with WHERE and ORDER BY.

  • USE – picks the database the next commands run in.
  • GO – ends a batch, so SQL Server runs everything above it first.
  • INSERT INTO … VALUES – adds new rows to a table. The brackets after the table name list the columns you fill.
  • SELECT * – reads every column. SELECT name, salary reads only those columns.
  • FROM – names the table to read from.
  • WHERE – keeps only the rows that match a condition, here salary > 500000.
  • ORDER BY – sorts the result. DESC means highest first; ASC (the default) means lowest first.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Insert

Write USE company_db; then GO. Insert IT and Human Resources into departments(department_name) in one statement. Then insert John, department 1, salary 800000 into employees(name, department_id, salary).

Select

Write SELECT * FROM employees;, then select name, salary where salary > 500000 ordered by salary DESC.

Step 8 Triggers

08_trigger.sql

SQL Server has no BEFORE trigger. An AFTER INSERT trigger fixes the row just after it is saved. The inserted table holds the new rows. A simpler way is a default: salary DECIMAL(10,2) DEFAULT 0.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Trigger

Write USE company_db; and GO. Create after_insert_employee ON employees AFTER INSERT AS. In BEGIN ... END update e setting e.salary = 0 from employees e joined to inserted i on e.id = i.id where i.salary IS NULL. End with GO.

12_joins.sql

Build on the departments and employees tables. First add a third table, projects.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Add a projects table

Write USE company_db; and GO. Create projects with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, project_name VARCHAR(80) and department_id INT FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES departments(id). Insert Payroll System (department 1) and Recruitment Drive (department 2) in one statement.

Step 12 Views in depth: change, depend, drop

13_views.sql

A view is only a stored query, so it depends on the tables underneath it.

Dependency: SQL Server lets you drop a table a view uses, and the view then fails. Create the view WITH SCHEMABINDING and SQL Server will refuse to drop the table under it.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Create a view over a join

Create dept_staff as the department-and-staff-count query (the GROUP BY query from Step 11), then select everything from it.

Change a view

Replace employee_view so it also shows department_id. SQL Server uses ALTER VIEW. End with GO.

What does a view depend on?

Select table_name from INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEW_TABLE_USAGE where view_name = 'employee_view'.

Drop a view

Write DROP VIEW dept_staff;.

Step 13 Roles in depth: revoke, nest, drop

14_roles.sql

Continue with the analyst user and the report_reader role from Step 5.

Role dependency: a role must have no members before you can drop it. The database user must be dropped before its login is no longer needed.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Take away a direct privilege

Write USE company_db;. Revoke SELECT ON SCHEMA::dbo from analyst. Then select dp.name AS role_name and m.name AS member_name from sys.database_role_members rm, joined to sys.database_principals dp on rm.role_principal_id = dp.principal_id and to sys.database_principals m on rm.member_principal_id = m.principal_id.

DENY beats GRANT

Write DENY SELECT ON dbo.employees TO analyst;. A deny wins over a grant from any role. Then REVOKE SELECT ON dbo.employees FROM analyst; removes the deny.

Clean up in order

Remove analyst from report_reader with ALTER ROLE ... DROP MEMBER, drop the role, drop the user. Then USE master; and drop the login.

Step 14 Triggers in depth: an audit log

15_audit_trigger.sql

Companies keep a record of who changed pay. A trigger can write that record automatically.

SQL Server has no OLD and NEW. It gives two virtual tables: deleted (the rows before) and inserted (the rows after). The trigger runs once per statement, not once per row, so it may see many rows.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Audit table

Write USE company_db; and GO. Create salary_audit with an identity id, employee_id INT, old_salary and new_salary (both DECIMAL(10,2)), and changed_at DATETIME DEFAULT GETDATE(). End with GO.

Audit trigger

Create after_update_salary ON employees AFTER UPDATE AS. In BEGIN ... END; insert into salary_audit (employee_id, old_salary, new_salary) the d.id, d.salary, i.salary from deleted d joined to inserted i on d.id = i.id where d.salary <> i.salary. End with GO.

Test and remove

Update John's salary to 900000, select everything from salary_audit, then DROP TRIGGER after_update_salary;.

Step 15 RPO and RTO: set a target, choose a backup plan

Two numbers decide your backup plan. RPO is how much data you can lose. RTO is how long you can be down. The business sets them, and you choose the tools to meet them.

TargetWhat it meansWhat you need
RPO 24 hoursYou can lose one day of data.One full backup every night.
RPO 1 hourYou can lose one hour.A nightly full backup plus log backups every hour.
RPO near 0You can lose almost nothing.A standby server that copies every change as it happens.
RTO 4 hoursBack online within 4 hours.Restore from backup, if a test restore proves it fits.
RTO 1 hourBack online within 1 hour.A fast restore (small database, fast disks), or a standby server.
RTO a few minutesAlmost no downtime.Automatic failover to a standby server.
Work it out. Your RTO is 1 hour. The database backup is 60 GB, the restore runs at 30 GB per hour, and checking the data takes 30 minutes. Real recovery time = restore (2 hours) + checking (30 minutes) = 2 hours 30 minutes. You miss the target. The fix is a smaller or faster restore, or a standby server. Rule: RPO = time since the last backup or log. RTO = time to detect + get a server + restore + check.

11_rpo.sql

Combine a full, a differential and a log backup. Then restore to a point in time with STOPAT. The paths are on the SQL Server machine.

Run the restore from master: USE master; first, because you cannot restore a database you are using. Time the restore: that is your real RTO.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Differential backup

Write BACKUP DATABASE company_db TO DISK = 'C:\Backup\company_diff.bak' WITH DIFFERENTIAL;. It saves only what changed since the last full backup.

Restore to a time

Restore the full backup WITH NORECOVERY, REPLACE. Then RESTORE LOG from C:\Backup\company_log.trn WITH STOPAT = '2026-10-26 09:59:00', RECOVERY;.

Step 16 Change data and tables

Interviewers often ask for the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP. You practise on a scratch table, temp_staff, so your real employees table stays safe.

CommandWhat it removesWHERE?Undo?
DELETEThe rows you choose, or all rows, one by one.YesYes, until you commit (see Step 18).
TRUNCATEEvery row at once. The table and its columns stay.NoYes, inside a transaction. It also restarts the IDENTITY counter.
DROP TABLEThe whole table: rows, columns and indexes.NoYes, inside a transaction you roll back. Otherwise restore from a backup.

16_change_data.sql

Change rows with UPDATE and DELETE, change the table with ALTER TABLE, then empty it and remove it.

Always write the WHERE. UPDATE or DELETE without it changes every row. Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to see which rows you will touch. TRUNCATE is refused when a foreign key in another table points at the table. A new column holds NULL (or its DEFAULT) in the old rows, and dropping a column deletes its data for good.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Scratch table

Write USE company_db; and GO first. Create temp_staff with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) and salary DECIMAL(10,2). Insert Amina 500000, Juma 600000 and Neema 700000 into temp_staff (name, salary) with one statement.

UPDATE

Raise Juma's salary by 10% with salary = salary * 1.10 and a WHERE on the name. Then select everything to see the change.

DELETE

Delete Neema with a WHERE, then select everything again.

ALTER TABLE

Add a column with ALTER TABLE temp_staff ADD phone VARCHAR(20);, then GO. Remove it with ALTER TABLE temp_staff DROP COLUMN phone;, then GO.

TRUNCATE and DROP

Empty the table with TRUNCATE TABLE temp_staff;, then remove the table itself with DROP TABLE temp_staff;.

Step 17 Constraints

A constraint is a rule the database enforces for you, so bad data cannot get in.

ConstraintWhat it doesIn this step
PRIMARY KEYIdentifies each row. Unique, never empty, one per table.id
FOREIGN KEYThe value must exist in another table.tasks.department_id
UNIQUENo two rows may share the value.email
NOT NULLThe value is required.name
CHECKThe value must pass a test.age >= 18
DEFAULTThe value used when you give none.status

When you run the three bad inserts, these are the errors to look for:

Rule brokenMessage (the wording may differ a little)
UNIQUEMsg 2627: Violation of UNIQUE KEY constraint ... Cannot insert duplicate key
NOT NULLMsg 515: Cannot insert the value NULL into column 'name'
CHECKMsg 547: The INSERT statement conflicted with the CHECK constraint

17_constraints.sql

Build a table with UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT, break each rule on purpose, then see ON DELETE CASCADE in action.

Foreign key behaviour. Without ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting a department that still has rows pointing at it is refused. With it, the child rows are deleted too. Use it only where that is what you mean: it can remove a lot of data with one statement.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Table with rules

Write USE company_db; and GO first. Create contacts with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, age INT CHECK (age >= 18) and status VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'active'.

A good row

Insert Amina (amina@example.com, age 30) giving only the email, name and age. Select everything: the status column was filled in by DEFAULT.

Three bad rows

Write three inserts that each break one rule, and watch each one fail: the same email again (UNIQUE), a row with no name (NOT NULL), and age 15 (CHECK). Use Juma 31, Neema 25 and Baraka 15.

Cascade table

Create tasks with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, department_id INT FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES departments(id) ON DELETE CASCADE and task VARCHAR(100).

Test the cascade

Insert a department called Temp. Insert one task for it with INSERT ... SELECT id, 'Test task' FROM departments WHERE .... Delete the department, then select everything from tasks: the task is gone too.

Clean up

Drop tasks, then contacts.

Step 18 Transactions

A transaction groups statements so they succeed or fail as one unit. The classic example is a bank transfer. ACID is the checklist interviewers expect.

LetterMeaningIn the bank transfer
A: AtomicityAll the changes in the transaction happen, or none do.Amina is never charged without Juma being paid.
C: ConsistencyThe data moves from one valid state to another. Constraints stay true.The total money in the two accounts stays the same.
I: IsolationTransactions running at the same time do not see each other's half-finished work.Another user never sees the money gone from Amina but not yet in Juma.
D: DurabilityAfter COMMIT the data survives a crash.The transfer is still there after a power cut.

Isolation levels say what one transaction may see of another. The table follows the SQL standard; real databases can be stricter.

Isolation levelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantom read
READ UNCOMMITTEDPossiblePossiblePossible
READ COMMITTEDNoPossiblePossible
REPEATABLE READNoNoPossible
SERIALIZABLENoNoNo

18_transactions.sql

Move money between two accounts, undo a mistake with ROLLBACK, undo only part of a transaction with a savepoint, and set an isolation level.

In this database. SQL Server runs READ COMMITTED by default and also offers SNAPSHOT. Each statement commits alone unless you BEGIN TRANSACTION. Add SET XACT_ABORT ON; in real code so a runtime error rolls the whole transaction back. Expected balances: after the transfer, Amina 800 and Juma 700. After the rollback they are the same. After the savepoint part, Amina 700 and Juma 800.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Accounts table

Write USE company_db; and GO first. Create accounts with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, owner VARCHAR(50) and balance DECIMAL(10,2). Insert Amina 1000 and Juma 500 in one statement.

Transfer and COMMIT

Move 200 from Amina to Juma as one transaction: begin with BEGIN TRANSACTION;, subtract 200 from Amina, add 200 to Juma, then COMMIT TRANSACTION;. Both changes are saved together.

A mistake and ROLLBACK

Begin again and subtract 900 from Amina. Select everything: her balance is now negative. Then ROLLBACK TRANSACTION; and select again: the change is gone.

SAVEPOINT

Begin, subtract 100 from Amina, then set a savepoint called after_debit. Add 1000 to Juma by mistake and go back to the savepoint with ROLLBACK TRANSACTION after_debit;. Add the right 100 to Juma and COMMIT TRANSACTION;.

Isolation level

Set SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;, then begin a transaction, select everything and commit it.

Clean up

Drop accounts.

Step 19 Monitoring and locks

A user phones: "the system is frozen". Usually one session holds a lock and others wait for it. You list the sessions, find who blocks whom, and end the blocker.

ProblemWhat you seeWhat you do
BlockingA query hangs, and blocking_session_id names the blockerKill the blocker, or ask its owner to commit.
DeadlockError 1205: Transaction was deadlocked ... and has been chosen as the deadlock victimSQL Server rolls the victim back for you. Run it again. The system_health event session records the deadlock graph.
Idle in a transactionA session did an update and never committed, so others wait on it.Ask the owner to commit or roll back. If you cannot, end the session.

Make a block on purpose (test server only), so you have something to find:

  1. In window 1 run BEGIN TRANSACTION; and UPDATE employees SET salary = salary WHERE name = 'John';. Do not commit.
  2. In window 2 run the same UPDATE. It waits.
  3. In window 3, as an admin, run the statements below, find window 1's session_id and kill it. Window 2 then finishes.

19_monitoring.sql

See who is connected, find the session that blocks the others, and end it.

Before you kill anything: look at what the session is doing and who owns it. A deadlock needs no kill: two sessions each wait for the other, so the database picks one as the victim and rolls it back. To avoid deadlocks, touch rows and tables in the same order everywhere and keep transactions short. Reading the sys.dm_ views needs the VIEW SERVER STATE permission. The older shortcut EXEC sp_who2; shows a BlkBy column that names the blocker. Killing a session rolls back its open transaction.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

List the sessions

Select session_id, login_name, status, host_name, program_name from sys.dm_exec_sessions where is_user_process = 1.

Find the blocker

Select session_id, blocking_session_id, wait_type, wait_time, command from sys.dm_exec_requests where blocking_session_id <> 0.

End the blocker

End the blocker with KILL 55;. Use the blocking_session_id you found in place of 55.

Locks that are waiting

Select request_session_id, resource_type, request_mode, request_status from sys.dm_tran_locks where request_status = 'WAIT'.

Step 20 Stored procedures

20_procedures.sql

A stored procedure is a named block of T-SQL saved inside the database. You run it with EXEC instead of retyping the statements.

  • CREATE PROCEDURE name @param TYPE – saves the procedure. Parameters start with @.
  • AS BEGIN … END – the statements the procedure runs.
  • @total INT OUTPUT – an output parameter that sends a value back.
  • GO – ends the batch. CREATE PROCEDURE must be the first statement in its batch.
  • EXEC / DECLARE – run a procedure / make a variable to catch the OUTPUT value.
  • sys.procedures / DROP PROCEDURE – list the procedures / delete one.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

raise_salary

Write USE company_db; and GO. Create raise_salary @dept INT, @pct DECIMAL(5,2) that multiplies salary by (1 + @pct / 100) for that department. End the batch with GO.

count_employees

Create count_employees @dept INT, @total INT OUTPUT that sets @total = COUNT(*) for the department. End with GO.

Call them

Run raise_salary with @dept = 1, @pct = 10. Declare @t INT, run count_employees with @total = @t OUTPUT, and select @t AS total.

List and drop

Select name, create_date from sys.procedures, then drop count_employees.

Step 21 Window functions

21_window_functions.sql

A window function calculates across related rows (a rank, a running total, the row before) and still shows every row.

  • OVER (...) – turns a function into a window function: it works across a set of rows but, unlike GROUP BY, keeps every row in the result.
  • ROW_NUMBER() – numbers the rows 1, 2, 3… with no ties.
  • RANK() / DENSE_RANK() – equal values share a rank. RANK then skips numbers (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2).
  • PARTITION BY – restarts the window for each group, here each department.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER – sets the order the window walks through the rows.
  • SUM() / AVG() OVER – a total or average shown next to every row.
  • LAG() / LEAD() – read the value from the row before / after.
  • ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW – the frame: from the first row up to this one, which makes a running total.
Interview favourite: "find the top earner in each department" (last part) and "RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER".

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Add sample rows

Write USE company_db; and GO, then add Mary (1, 900000), Peter (1, 700000), Asha (2, 600000) and Neema (2, 650000) in one INSERT.

Rank everyone

Select name, department_id, salary with ROW_NUMBER() as row_num, RANK() as rnk and DENSE_RANK() as dense_rnk, all OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC).

Per department

Add PARTITION BY department_id: RANK() by salary as dept_rank, SUM(salary) as dept_total and AVG(salary) as dept_avg.

Previous, next, running total

Ordered by salary: LAG(salary) as prev_salary, LEAD(salary) as next_salary, and a running SUM(salary) with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW as running_total.

Top earner per department

In a subquery ranked, number rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn. Outside, keep rn = 1.

  • Run SELECT name FROM sys.tables;. You should see departments and employees.
  • Run the JOIN. John shows with IT.
  • Connect as analyst: SELECT works, DELETE FROM employees; fails with "permission denied".
  • Back up, delete a row, restore with WITH REPLACE, and confirm the row is back.
  • Insert an employee with no salary. The trigger stores 0.
  • Run the LEFT JOIN. Human Resources appears with an empty name, and the three-table join lists John with IT and Payroll System.
  • Run SELECT name FROM sys.tables;. The scratch table temp_staff is gone after Step 16.
  • In Step 17 each of the three bad inserts fails with its own error, and SELECT * FROM tasks; returns no rows after the department is deleted.
  • In Step 18 the balances end at Amina 700 and Juma 800, and the 900 subtraction leaves no trace after the rollback.
  • In Step 19 window 2's UPDATE waits until you end window 1's session, then it finishes.
  • Run CALL raise_salary(1, 10); (Oracle and SQL Server: EXEC). The salaries in department 1 go up by 10%.
  • Run the window queries. Every employee still appears, with a rank, the department total next to each row, and one top earner per department in the last query.

Interview questions

What is a view, and why use it?

A view is a saved SELECT that you query like a table. It stores no data of its own. Use it to hide columns (for example salary), to give users a simpler picture of the data, and to reuse a long query.

Why create an index?

An index lets the database find rows without reading the whole table, so searches, joins and sorting on that column are faster. The cost: it uses disk space and makes INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE a little slower.

What are RPO and RTO?

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how long the system may stay down. Example: RPO = 15 minutes, RTO = 1 hour.

The server crashes at 10:00 and backups run every 15 minutes. What is the RPO?

The most you can lose is 15 minutes of data, because the last backup could have been taken at 09:45. To lower the RPO you back up more often or add log-based recovery (see the recovery step).

A query WHERE name='John' is slow. What do you do?

Check the execution plan to see if it scans the whole table. Create an index on name. Select only the columns you need instead of *. Then check the plan again.

What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?

DELETE removes the rows you choose and accepts a WHERE. TRUNCATE empties the whole table quickly and keeps its structure. DROP TABLE removes the table itself. Whether you can undo them depends on the database and on whether you are inside a transaction.

How do you add or remove a column on a table that already has data?

ALTER TABLE with an add or a DROP COLUMN clause. Old rows get NULL or the DEFAULT in a new column. Dropping a column deletes its data, so take a backup first.

What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE?

A table has one primary key, it identifies each row, and it can never be empty. A table can have many UNIQUE constraints, and in most databases a unique column may hold NULL.

What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?

When you delete a parent row, the database deletes the child rows that point at it. Without it, deleting a parent that still has children is refused.

What does ACID mean?

Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: the data stays valid. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work. Durability: committed data survives a crash.

What is the difference between COMMIT and ROLLBACK?

COMMIT makes the changes of the transaction permanent. ROLLBACK undoes them. A savepoint lets you undo only the part after it.

What are the isolation levels?

From weakest to strongest: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE. A stronger level prevents more problems (dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads) but allows less concurrency.

Users say the database is frozen. What do you do?

List the sessions, find the one that blocks the others (sys.dm_exec_requests (the blocking_session_id column) or sp_who2, then KILL), check what it is doing and who owns it, and ask the owner to commit. If that is not possible, end the session.

What is a deadlock and how do you avoid it?

Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can move. The database ends one as the victim. Avoid it by accessing tables and rows in the same order and keeping transactions short.

The big question. One realistic ticket that needs everything from the other steps: tables and constraints, data, joins, a view, users, an index, a trigger, a transaction, a backup, a recovery plan and a frozen system. You analyse it first, then build it file by file. Finish the other steps in this database first, or use them as a reference.

Practise on a test server only. This creates a new database called shop_db (separate from company_db), users and a backup. Never run it on a live system, and never type a real password into this page.

Question:

Database for this question:

Step 1 Read the question and plan

The ticket from the shop manager. You are the new DBA at KijijiShop, a small online shop. Build its database, shop_db.
  1. Store customers (name, a unique email, phone), products (name, category, a price above zero, stock that never goes below zero), orders (customer, status that starts as "new", date) and the items of each order (product, quantity above zero, the price at the time). Deleting an order must delete its items.
  2. Load sample data: 3 customers, 4 products, 2 orders with their items.
  3. Raise the price of every "Drinks" product by 10%. Delete the cancelled order. Add a loyalty_points column to customers, starting at 0.
  4. Reports: each order with the customer name and its total; customers who never ordered; categories with revenue above 2000; products nobody has bought.
  5. The sales team must not see customer emails: give them a view of order totals and a read-only user. A clerk user may add and change orders, but not delete anything.
  6. Orders are searched by date all day: make that fast.
  7. Every price change must be recorded: who it was, the old price and the new price.
  8. Placing an order must be all or nothing: the order, its items and the stock change are saved together, or none of them is.
  9. Take a backup, and prove you can restore it.
  10. The business wants to lose at most 1 hour of data and be back within 1 hour. What backup plan do you need?
  11. Monday morning the shop is frozen. What do you do?

Method: how to attack a big question

  1. Read the whole ticket once before you type anything.
  2. Underline the nouns. They become tables and columns. Underline the verbs and the rules ("never", "must", "only"). They become statements and constraints.
  3. Draw the relationships. Where a thing "has many" of another, the many side gets a foreign key. Where both sides have many, add a table in the middle.
  4. Order the work by what depends on what. Parent tables before child tables, tables before data, data before reports, reports before the view that uses them.
  5. Write one file for each group of lines, run it, and check the result with a SELECT before moving on.
  6. Answer the lines that are not code (backup plan, a frozen system) in plain words, with the exact commands you would use.

The design that falls out of line 1

RelationshipKindHow you build it
customers and ordersOne customer has many ordersA foreign key orders.customer_id
orders and order_itemsOne order has many itemsA foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE
products and order_itemsOne product appears in many itemsA foreign key order_items.product_id
orders and productsMany to manySolved by the order_items table in the middle
Why unit_price is stored on each item. Prices change (line 3 raises them). An old order must still show what the customer actually paid, so the item keeps a copy of the price from the day of the order. Without it, a price rise would silently change old totals.

Step 2 Build the tables

01_shop_create.sql

Turn the nouns and rules of line 1 into four tables.

Every rule from line 1 of the ticket is a constraint in the table, so bad data can never get in. Create the parent tables first: a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Database

Create the database shop_db and switch to it with USE shop_db;.

customers

Create customers with id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE and phone VARCHAR(20).

Customers and products

03_shop_reports.sql

Line 4 of the ticket: four reports with joins, grouping and a subquery.

Expected results: order 1 for Amina totals 4200. Juma and Neema never ordered (Juma's only order was cancelled and deleted). Only Drinks passes the 2000 line (3000). Juice and Rice 5kg were never bought. A HAVING filters groups after the sum, a WHERE filters rows before it.

Order totals

Write USE shop_db; first. Select o.id, the customer c.name and SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) as total from orders o. Add JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id and JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id, then GROUP BY o.id, c.name.

That is normal: the index pays off when the table has thousands of rows. The trigger logs only real price changes, so the stock updates in Step 7 add nothing to the audit.

Create price_audit with id, product_id, old_price and new_price, and a changed_at timestamp that defaults to now.

Audit trigger

Create after_update_price AFTER UPDATE ON products FOR EACH ROW that inserts OLD.id, OLD.price, NEW.price into price_audit (product_id, old_price, new_price), but only WHERE OLD.price <> NEW.price, so stock changes are not logged.

Test it

Set Cola's price to 1700, then select everything from price_audit. One row shows 1650 and 1700.

Step 7 Place an order safely

06_shop_order.sql

Line 8 of the ticket: an order, its items and the stock change are saved together or not at all.

Expected: two orders remain (1 and the good new one), and Rice 5kg stock is 18. MAX(id) finds the new order on a practice server with one user. In a real application read the new id with LAST_INSERT_ID().

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

A good order

Write USE shop_db; first. Begin with START TRANSACTION;. Insert an order for customer 3 ('new', '2026-10-05'). Insert its item with INSERT ... SELECT (SELECT MAX(id) FROM orders), id, 2, price FROM products WHERE name = 'Rice 5kg', so the order id and the price come from the data. Take 2 off the stock of Rice 5kg, then COMMIT;.

An order that must fail

Begin again. Insert an order for customer 3 dated '2026-10-06', insert an item for 100 Rice 5kg, then take 100 off the stock. The stock CHECK (stock >= 0) stops that last statement. Finish with ROLLBACK; so the order and the item disappear.

Check the result

Select everything from orders, then name and stock from products.

Step 8 Backup and restore

terminal

Line 9 of the ticket: take a backup and prove you can restore it.

A backup you have never restored is only a hope. Drop one order row, restore, and check it is back. Time the restore: that time is your real RTO.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Back up

Dump shop_db with mysqldump -u root -p into shop_backup.sql.

Restore

Load the file back into shop_db with mysql -u root -p shop_db < shop_backup.sql.

Step 9 Answer the last lines in words

Lines 10 and 11 have no code to type. In an interview you answer them out loud, so practise saying them. Open each answer only after you have tried.

Line 10: lose at most 1 hour, back within 1 hour. What plan do you need?

RPO 1 hour needs more than a nightly backup: a nightly full backup plus the binary log (point-in-time recovery with mysqlbinlog), taken at least every hour. RTO 1 hour means the restore must finish in an hour, so time a real restore. If the database is too big to restore in time, make the backup smaller or faster, or keep a standby server. The business sets the two numbers; you choose the tools.

Line 11: the shop is frozen. What do you do?

Do not restart anything yet. Look at the sessions, find the one that blocks the others (SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST and sys.innodb_lock_waits to find the blocker, then KILL it), check what it is doing and who owns it, and ask the owner to commit. If that fails, end that one session. Then find out why it held the lock so far (a forgotten open transaction, a long job) and fix the cause.

Walk me through your design.

Four tables. customers and products are the things. orders belongs to one customer. order_items sits between orders and products because an order has many products and a product is in many orders. Each rule from the ticket is a constraint, so the data protects itself.

Why does an order item store the price?

Prices change. The item keeps the price from the day of the order, so old orders and reports still show what the customer paid.

Why is placing an order a transaction?

It changes three things: the order, its items and the stock. If one fails, the others must be undone, or the shop would sell stock it does not have. That is atomicity.

How do you make sure the clerk cannot delete anything?

Grant only SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE on the tables the job needs, and never DELETE. Nobody gets more than the job needs.

Step 10 Check that it worked

  • Run SHOW TABLES; in shop_db. You should see customers, products, orders, order_items, price_audit and the view order_summary.
  • Insert a customer with an email that already exists, and a product with price 0. Both must fail.
  • The order report shows order 1 for Amina with a total of 4200.
  • Connect as shop_reader: SELECT * FROM order_summary; works, but SELECT * FROM customers; on customers fails.
  • Change a product price: a row appears in price_audit with the old and new price.
  • The failing 100-rice order leaves no new order, and the Rice 5kg stock is 18.
  • Take the backup, delete a row, restore, and confirm the row is back.

Step 1 Read the question and plan

The ticket from the shop manager. You are the new DBA at KijijiShop, a small online shop. Build its database, shop_db.
  1.   8. Placing an order must be all or nothing: the order, its items and the stock change are saved together, or none of them is.
  9. Take a backup, and prove you can restore it.

  11. Monday morning the shop is frozen. What do you do?

Method: how to attack a big question

  1. Read the whole ticket once before you type anything.
  2. Underline the nouns. They become tables and columns. Underline the verbs and the rules ("never", "must", "only"). They become statements and constraints.
  3. Draw the relationships. Where a thing "has many" of another, the many side gets a foreign key. Where both sides have many, add a table in the middle.
  4. Order the work by what depends on what. Parent tables before child tables, tables before data, data before reports, reports before the view that uses them.
  5. Write one file for each group of lines, run it, and check the result with a SELECT before moving on.
  6. Answer the lines that are not code (backup plan, a frozen system) in plain words, with the exact commands you would use.

01_shop_create.sql

Every rule from line 1 of the ticket is a constraint in the table, so bad data can never get in. Create the parent tables first: a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Database

Create the database shop_db and switch to it with \c shop_db.

customers

Create customers with id INT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE and phone VARCHAR(20).

products

Create products with the id, name, category, a price that must be above zero, and a stock that defaults to 0 and may not go below zero.

orders

Create orders with the id, customer_id (required, a foreign key to customers(id)), status (required, default 'new') and order_date (a DATE).

order_items

Create order_items with the id, order_id (a foreign key to orders(id) with ON DELETE CASCADE), product_id (a foreign key to products(id)), quantity (above zero) and unit_price (required).

02_shop_data.sql

Customers and products

You are connected to shop_db. Insert Amina, Juma and Neema (name, email, phone), then Cola and Juice (Drinks, 1500 and 2000, stock 50 and 30), Bread (Food, 1200, stock 40) and Rice 5kg (Food, 9000, stock 20). One statement for each table.

Orders and items

Insert order 1 (customer 1, 'paid', 2026-10-01) and order 2 (customer 2, 'cancelled', 2026-10-02). Then the items: order 1 has Cola x2 at 1500 and Bread x1 at 1200; order 2 has Juice x1 at 2000.

Price rise and cancelled order

Raise Drinks prices by 10% with price = price * 1.10. Delete the cancelled order with a WHERE on status. Then select everything from order_items: the cancelled order's item is gone too.

New column

Add loyalty_points to customers as INT with DEFAULT 0.

Step 4 Reports

03_shop_reports.sql

Line 4 of the ticket: four reports with joins, grouping and a subquery.

Expected results: order 1 for Amina totals 4200. Juma and Neema never ordered (Juma's only order was cancelled and deleted). Only Drinks passes the 2000 line (3000). Juice and Rice 5kg were never bought. A HAVING filters groups after the sum, a WHERE filters rows before it.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Order totals

You are connected to shop_db. Select o.id, the customer c.name and SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) as total from orders o. Add JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id and JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id, then GROUP BY o.id, c.name.

Customers who never ordered

Select c.name from customers c with a LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id on orders, keeping only the rows where o.id IS NULL.

Revenue above 2000

Select p.category and SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) as revenue from order_items i joined to products p. Group by category and keep only groups with HAVING SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) > 2000.

Products nobody bought

Select name from products where id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items).

Create shop_clerk the same way with CONNECT and USAGE. Grant SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE on orders, SELECT, INSERT on order_items, and SELECT, UPDATE on products. No DELETE anywhere.

SELECT (SELECT MAX(id) FROM orders), id, 2, price FROM products WHERE name = 'Rice 5kg', so the order id and the price come from the data. Take 2 off the stock of Rice 5kg, then COMMIT;.

An order that must fail

Begin again. Insert an order for customer 3 dated DATE '2026-10-06', insert an item for 100 Rice 5kg, then take 100 off the stock. The stock CHECK (stock >= 0) stops that last statement. Finish with ROLLBACK; so the order and the item disappear.

Check the result

Select everything from orders, then name and stock from products.

Step 8 Backup and restore

terminal

Line 9 of the ticket: take a backup and prove you can restore it.

A backup you have never restored is only a hope. Drop one order row, restore, and check it is back. Time the restore: that time is your real RTO.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Back up

Export the schema with expdp system@localhost/XEPDB1 schemas=shop_db directory=DATA_PUMP_DIR dumpfile=shop_db.dmp logfile=shop_db_exp.log into shop_db.dmp.

Restore

Import it with impdp, adding table_exists_action=replace.

Step 9 Answer the last lines in words

Lines 10 and 11 have no code to type. In an interview you answer them out loud, so practise saying them. Open each answer only after you have tried.

Line 10: lose at most 1 hour, back within 1 hour. What plan do you need?

RPO 1 hour needs more than a nightly backup: a nightly full backup plus archived redo logs backed up with RMAN, taken at least every hour. RTO 1 hour means the restore must finish in an hour, so time a real restore. If the database is too big to restore in time, make the backup smaller or faster, or keep a standby server. The business sets the two numbers; you choose the tools.

Line 11: the shop is frozen. What do you do?

Do not restart anything yet. Look at the sessions, find the one that blocks the others (v$session and its blocking_session column, then ALTER SYSTEM KILL SESSION), check what it is doing and who owns it, and ask the owner to commit. If that fails, end that one session. Then find out why it held the lock so far (a forgotten open transaction, a long job) and fix the cause.

Walk me through your design.

Four tables. customers and products are the things. orders belongs to one customer. order_items sits between orders and products because an order has many products and a product is in many orders. Each rule from the ticket is a constraint, so the data protects itself.

Why does an order item store the price?

Prices change. The item keeps the price from the day of the order, so old orders and reports still show what the customer paid.

Why is placing an order a transaction?

It changes three things: the order, its items and the stock. If one fails, the others must be undone, or the shop would sell stock it does not have. That is atomicity.

How do you make sure the clerk cannot delete anything?

Grant only SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE on the tables the job needs, and never DELETE. Nobody gets more than the job needs.

Step 10 Check that it worked

  • Run SELECT table_name FROM user_tables; in shop_db. You should see customers, products, orders, order_items, price_audit and the view order_summary.
  • Insert a customer with an email that already exists, and a product with price 0. Both must fail.
  • The order report shows order 1 for Amina with a total of 4200.
  • Connect as shop_reader: SELECT * FROM order_summary; works, but SELECT * FROM customers; on customers fails.
  • Change a product price: a row appears in price_audit with the old and new price.
  • The failing 100-rice order leaves no new order, and the Rice 5kg stock is 18.
  • Take the backup, delete a row, restore, and confirm the row is back.

The big question. One realistic ticket that needs everything from the other steps: tables and constraints, data, joins, a view, users, an index, a trigger, a transaction, a backup, a recovery plan and a frozen system. You analyse it first, then build it file by file. Finish the other steps in this database first, or use them as a reference.

Practise on a test server only. This creates a new database called shop_db (separate from company_db), users and a backup. Never run it on a live system, and never type a real password into this page.

Step 1 Read the question and plan

The ticket from the shop manager. You are the new DBA at KijijiShop, a small online shop. Build its database, shop_db.
  1. Store customers (name, a unique email, phone), products (name, category, a price above zero, stock that never goes below zero), orders (customer, status that starts as "new", date) and the items of each order (product, quantity above zero, the price at the time). Deleting an order must delete its items.
  2. Load sample data: 3 customers, 4 products, 2 orders with their items.
  3. Raise the price of every "Drinks" product by 10%. Delete the cancelled order. Add a loyalty_points column to customers, starting at 0.

  5. The sales team must not see customer emails: give them a view of order totals and a read-only user. A clerk user may add and change orders, but not delete anything.

  7. Every price change must be recorded: who it was, the old price and the new price.
  8. Placing an order must be all or nothing: the order, its items and the stock change are saved together, or none of them is.
  9. Take a backup, and prove you can restore it.
  10. The business wants to lose at most 1 hour of data and be back within 1 hour. What backup plan do you need?
  11. Monday morning the shop is frozen. What do you do?

Method: how to attack a big question

  1. Read the whole ticket once before you type anything.
  2. Underline the nouns. They become tables and columns. Underline the verbs and the rules ("never", "must", "only"). They become statements and constraints.
  3. Draw the relationships. Where a thing "has many" of another, the many side gets a foreign key. Where both sides have many, add a table in the middle.
  4. Order the work by what depends on what. Parent tables before child tables, tables before data, data before reports, reports before the view that uses them.
  5. Write one file for each group of lines, run it, and check the result with a SELECT before moving on.
  6. Answer the lines that are not code (backup plan, a frozen system) in plain words, with the exact commands you would use.

The design that falls out of line 1

RelationshipKindHow you build it
customers and ordersOne customer has many ordersA foreign key orders.customer_id
orders and order_itemsOne order has many itemsA foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE
products and order_itemsOne product appears in many itemsA foreign key order_items.product_id
orders and productsMany to manySolved by the order_items table in the middle
Why unit_price is stored on each item. Prices change (line 3 raises them). An old order must still show what the customer actually paid, so the item keeps a copy of the price from the day of the order. Without it, a price rise would silently change old totals.

01_shop_create.sql

Every rule from line 1 of the ticket is a constraint in the table, so bad data can never get in. Create the parent tables first: a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Database

Create the database shop_db, then GO. Switch to it with USE shop_db;, then GO.

customers

Create customers with id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE and phone VARCHAR(20).

products

orders

Create orders with the id, customer_id (required, a foreign key to customers(id)), status (required, default 'new') and order_date (a DATE).

order_items

Create order_items with the id, order_id (a foreign key to orders(id) with ON DELETE CASCADE), product_id (a foreign key to products(id)), quantity (above zero) and unit_price (required).

Order totals

Write USE shop_db; and GO first. Select o.id, the customer c.name and SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) as total from orders o. Add JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id and JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id, then GROUP BY o.id, c.name.

Customers who never ordered

Select c.name from customers c with a LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id on orders, keeping only the rows where o.id IS NULL.

Revenue above 2000

Products nobody bought

Select name from products where id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items).

Create the login shop_reader with PASSWORD = 'Str0ng_Pass!', the user shop_reader for that login, and grant SELECT on order_summary only.

Do the same for shop_clerk. Grant SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE on orders, SELECT, INSERT on order_items, and SELECT, UPDATE on products. No DELETE anywhere.

Big question: a government recruitment portal. This is Task 1 from your question sheet: a database for an online job portal where applicants apply for public-service vacancies, get shortlisted, sit interviews and are placed. You build the schema, seed it, answer every question on the sheet, add an index and an audit trigger, and show one applicant's whole journey. Every query here is written for MySQL.

Practise on a test server only. This creates a new database called recruit_db, an audit table and a trigger. Never run it on a live system, and never type a real password or a real National ID into this page.

Question:

Database for this question:

Step 1 Read the question and plan

Task 1, as given. Tables: Applicants (ApplicantID, FullName, Email, Phone, NationalID, PasswordHash, RegistrationDate), Applications (ApplicationID, ApplicantID, VacancyID, AppliedDate, ApplicationStatus, ShortlistStatus, LastUpdated), Vacancies (VacancyID, JobTitle, PublicInstitution, Cadre, NumberOfPosts, AdvertDate, ClosingDate, Status), Placements (PlacementID, ApplicationID, Institution, PlacementDate, PlacementStatus) and InterviewResults (ResultID, ApplicationID, InterviewType, InterviewDate, Score, ResultStatus).
  1. Section A.1 Create the schema with data types, primary keys, foreign keys, unique NationalID and Email, one application per applicant per vacancy, CHECK constraints on status fields, and indexes on the columns the API filters and joins on. Supply it as schema.sql.
  2. Section A.2 Seed at least 10 realistic records per major table: vacancies that are Open, Closed and past their closing date; applicants with and without applications; at least one applicant who reached placement.
  3. i Total successfully submitted applications. ii Average applications per vacancy, including vacancies with zero. iii / Q3 Vacancies that never received an application. iv / Q4 Vacancies still Open after their closing date. v / Q2 Top five vacancies with their rank. vi Recruitment funnel per public institution. vii Overall placement rate. viii / Q5 Vacancy with the most applications.
  4. Joins: Q1 applicants with submitted applications, Q6 name, vacancy, date and status, Q7 shortlisted applicants, Q8 interview totals, Q9 more than one vacancy, Q10 never submitted, Q11 selected but not placed.
  5. x / Q12 Show a complete application journey.
  6. Index joins / Q12 practical: create an index on applications(vacancy_id) and compare the execution plan before and after.
  7. ix / Q13: an audit table and a trigger that records application status changes.

The sheet numbers some questions twice (i to x, then Q1 to Q13). This table puts each one in a single file, so nothing is done twice.

Joins, Q1, Q6 to Q11JOIN, LEFT JOIN, NOT EXISTS, GROUP BY ... HAVING06_joins.sql7

The design

APPLICANTS 1 ───< APPLICATIONS >─── 1 VACANCIES
                       │ 1
             ┌─────────┴──────────┐
             *                   0..1
     INTERVIEW_RESULTS        PLACEMENTS

UNIQUE (applicant_id, vacancy_id)   one application per applicant per vacancy
UNIQUE (placements.application_id)  an application is placed at most once
One rule to agree before any query: what counts as "submitted"? In this design an application is submitted when its status is Submitted, Selected or Rejected. A Draft was never sent, and a Withdrawn was pulled back. Every report below uses that same list, so the numbers agree with each other. Write the definition down in an interview: it shows you asked what the business means.

Step 2 schema.sql: tables, keys and rules

schema.sql

Section A.1. Each rule in the question becomes a constraint, so bad data cannot get in. Parent tables come first, because a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Constraint names such as uq_app_once make error messages readable and let you drop a rule later. UNIQUE (applicant_id, vacancy_id) already gives an index on applicant_id, because applicant_id starts with that column. MySQL already builds an index for every foreign key, so interview_results.application_id and applications.vacancy_id are indexed for free. A separate index on applications.vacancy_id is left out on purpose: you add it in Step 9 and measure the difference.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Database

Create the database recruit_db and switch to it with USE recruit_db;.

applicants

Create applicants with an identity applicant_id, full_name, email, phone, national_id, password_hash and registration_date DATE. Make email and national_id unique with named constraints.

vacancies

Create vacancies with the id, job_title, public_institution, cadre, number_of_posts (above zero), advert_date, closing_date (not before the advert date) and status ('Open' or 'Closed', default 'Open').

applications

Create applications with the id, applicant_id and vacancy_id (both required foreign keys), applied_date, application_status (Draft, Submitted, Withdrawn, Selected, Rejected), shortlist_status (Pending, Shortlisted, Not Shortlisted) and last_updated. Add UNIQUE on (applicant_id, vacancy_id).

interview_results

Create interview_results with the id, application_id (foreign key), interview_type (Written, Oral, Practical), interview_date, score from 0 to 100, and result_status (Passed or Failed).

placements

Create placements with the id, application_id (foreign key, unique), institution, placement_date and placement_status (Placed, Reported, Declined; default Placed).

Indexes

Index the columns the API filters on: idx_vac_status_close on vacancies (status, closing_date), idx_vac_institution on vacancies (public_institution), and idx_app_status on applications (application_status).

Seed data is not random: each row is there to make one question return something you can check. The table shows what each special row is for.

seed.sql

Section A.2. Run it once on the fresh schema, so the ids start at 1: the applications refer to applicants and vacancies by those ids.

The password hashes are fake placeholders: a real system stores a bcrypt or Argon2 hash made by the application, never a password. Placements has only 2 rows on purpose: only selected applicants can be placed, and Q11 needs one selected applicant who is not placed yet. The dates are set around October 2026, so question iv depends on today's date when you run it.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Vacancies

Write USE recruit_db; first. Insert the 10 vacancies into vacancies (job title, institution, cadre, posts, advert date, closing date, status), one statement with one row per line. Copy them from the full code above.

Applicants

Insert the 12 applicants (name, email, phone, a 20-digit National ID, a fake password hash and the registration date).

Applications

Insert the 15 applications as (applicant_id, vacancy_id, applied_date, application_status, shortlist_status). Check that no pair repeats, or uq_app_once stops the insert.

Interview results

Insert the 10 interview results for the shortlisted applications: type, date, score and Passed or Failed.

Placements

Step 4 The headline numbers

03_kpis.sql

Questions i, ii and vii.

Expected: 13 submitted applications, an average of 1.30 per vacancy (13 over 10 vacancies) and a placement rate of 15.38% (2 of 13). The status filter for ii sits in the ON condition, not in WHERE: a WHERE would throw away the vacancies with zero applications, and the average would wrongly become 13 over 7. * 1.0 turns whole-number division into decimal division on every database.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

i. Submitted applications

Write USE recruit_db; first. Count the rows in applications whose status is in ('Submitted', 'Selected', 'Rejected'), named submitted_applications.

ii. Average per vacancy

In a derived table per_vacancy, count submitted applications for every vacancy with vacancies v LEFT JOIN applications a, keeping the status test inside the ON. Outside, take AVG(app_count * 1.0), rounded to 2 places.

vii. Placement rate

From submitted applications a LEFT JOIN placements p, divide COUNT(p.placement_id) by COUNT(a.application_id), times 100.0, rounded to 2 places.

Step 5 Vacancy reports

04_vacancy_reports.sql

Questions iii/Q3, iv/Q4, v/Q2 and viii/Q5.

Expected: iii returns vacancies 8, 9 and 10. iv returns 6 and 7 (on 2026-10-26; later dates add more). v returns seven rows, not five: Accountant II and Nurse Officer II tie on 3 and both get rank 1, then two vacancies share rank 3 and three share rank 5. RANK() keeps ties honest; ROW_NUMBER() would cut them at random and DENSE_RANK() would give 1, 1, 2, 2, 3. viii returns the same two leaders, because a maximum can be shared. CURRENT_DATE gets today's date in MySQL.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

iii. Never received an application

Write USE recruit_db; first. Select the vacancy id, title, institution and status from vacancies v, LEFT JOIN applications a on the vacancy id, keeping rows where a.application_id IS NULL.

iv. Open after closing date

Select id, title and closing date from vacancies where status = 'Open' and closing_date < CURRENT_DATE.

v. Top five with rank

In a derived table ranked, count submitted applications per vacancy and add RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(a.application_id) DESC) AS rnk. Outside, keep rnk <= 5 and order by rnk, vacancy_id.

viii. The maximum

Count submitted applications per vacancy and keep the groups whose count equals MAX(cnt) of the per-vacancy counts, using HAVING.

Step 6 The recruitment funnel

05_funnel.sql

Question vi: per public institution, how many applications go in at the top, and how many survive each stage.

Why DISTINCT? An application with two interview rows appears twice after the join, so a plain COUNT would count Amina twice. COUNT(DISTINCT ...) counts it once. CASE ... END returns NULL when the condition is false, and COUNT ignores NULLs, so each column counts only its own stage. Expected: Ministry of Finance 3, 2, 1, 1; Office of the Attorney General 1, 1, 1, 1; e-Government Authority 2, 2, 1, 0.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Funnel query

Write USE recruit_db; first. Group by v.public_institution. Count distinct submitted applications, distinct shortlisted ones, distinct ones with a 'Passed' interview, and distinct placed ones. Join applications, then LEFT JOIN interview_results and placements.

Step 7 Join questions

06_joins.sql

Q1 and Q6 to Q11. Each one practises a different kind of join.

Interview questions

Why is "one application per applicant per vacancy" a UNIQUE constraint and not a check in the API?

Two requests can arrive at the same moment, and both API checks would pass. A UNIQUE on (applicant_id, vacancy_id) is enforced by the database itself, so the second insert always fails. The API can still check first to show a friendly message.

Why does the average per vacancy use a LEFT JOIN?

An inner join drops vacancies with no applications, so they would vanish from the average and make it look higher. The LEFT JOIN keeps them with a count of 0. The status filter must sit in the ON, or a WHERE would remove those rows again.

How would you fix vacancies that are still Open after closing?

Close them with UPDATE vacancies SET status = 'Closed' WHERE status = 'Open' AND closing_date < CURRENT_DATE;, and run it every night as a MySQL EVENT. Better still, compute "open" from the dates when you read, so the flag can never be wrong.

RANK, DENSE_RANK or ROW_NUMBER for a top five?

RANK gives ties the same rank and skips numbers (1, 1, 3). DENSE_RANK does not skip (1, 1, 2). ROW_NUMBER gives every row a different number and breaks ties at random. For "top five vacancies" RANK is the fair choice, and you say that ties may return more than five rows.

Why COUNT(DISTINCT ...) in the funnel?

Joining interview results multiplies rows: an applicant with two interviews appears twice. Counting distinct application ids counts each application once per stage.

Why index foreign key columns?

Joins and filters use them all the time, and deleting a parent row has to search the child table. MySQL indexes them automatically.

Why audit with a trigger instead of in the application code?

The trigger fires for every update, from the API, a script, or a DBA at the console, so nothing escapes the log. It runs inside the same transaction, so if the update rolls back, the audit row does too.

Why store a password hash and not the password?

If the database leaks, a slow salted hash such as bcrypt cannot be turned back into the password. The application hashes the password at registration and compares hashes at login; the database never sees the real password.

The design

APPLICANTS 1 ───< APPLICATIONS >─── 1 VACANCIES
                       │ 1
             ┌─────────┴──────────┐
             *                   0..1
     INTERVIEW_RESULTS        PLACEMENTS

UNIQUE (applicant_id, vacancy_id)   one application per applicant per vacancy

One rule to agree before any query: what counts as "submitted"? In this design an application is submitted when its status is Submitted, Selected or Rejected. A Draft was never sent, and a Withdrawn was pulled back. Every report below uses that same list, so the numbers agree with each other. Write the definition down in an interview: it shows you asked what the business means.

Step 2 schema.sql: tables, keys and rules

schema.sql

Section A.1. Each rule in the question becomes a constraint, so bad data cannot get in. Parent tables come first, because a foreign key needs its target to exist.

Constraint names such as uq_app_once make error messages readable and let you drop a rule later. UNIQUE (applicant_id, vacancy_id) already gives an index on applicant_id, because applicant_id starts with that column. PostgreSQL does not index foreign key columns for you, so interview_results.application_id gets its own index. applications.vacancy_id is left out on purpose: you add it in Step 9 and measure the difference.

Read the full code

Practise it part by part

Database

Create the database recruit_db and connect to it with \c recruit_db.

applicants

Create applicants with an identity applicant_id, full_name, email, phone, national_id, password_hash and registration_date DATE. Make email and national_id unique with named constraints.

vacancies

Create vacancies with the id, job_title, public_institution, cadre, number_of_posts (above zero), advert_date, closing_date (not before the advert date) and status ('Open' or 'Closed', default 'Open').

applications

Create applications with the id, applicant_id and vacancy_id (both required foreign keys), applied_date, application_status (Draft, Submitted, Withdrawn, Selected, Rejected), shortlist_status (Pending, Shortlisted, Not Shortlisted) and last_updated. Add UNIQUE on (applicant_id, vacancy_id).

interview_results

Create interview_results with the id, application_id (foreign key), interview_type (Written, Oral, Practical), interview_date, score from 0 to 100, and result_status (Passed or Failed).

placements

Create placements with the id, application_id (foreign key, unique), institution, placement_date and placement_status (Placed, Reported, Declined; default Placed).

Indexes

Index the columns the API filters on: idx_vac_status_close on vacancies (status, closing_date), idx_vac_institution on vacancies (public_institution), and idx_app_status on applications (application_status). Also idx_result_app on interview_results (application_id).

Interview questions

Why is "one application per applicant per vacancy" a UNIQUE constraint and not a check in the API?

Two requests can arrive at the same moment, and both API checks would pass. A UNIQUE on (applicant_id, vacancy_id) is enforced by the database itself, so the second insert always fails. The API can still check first to show a friendly message.

Why does the average per vacancy use a LEFT JOIN?

An inner join drops vacancies with no applications, so they would vanish from the average and make it look higher. The LEFT JOIN keeps them with a count of 0. The status filter must sit in the ON, or a WHERE would remove those rows again.

How would you fix vacancies that are still Open after closing?

Close them with UPDATE vacancies SET status = 'Closed' WHERE status = 'Open' AND closing_date < CURRENT_DATE;, and run it every night as pg_cron or an operating-system cron job. Better still, compute "open" from the dates when you read, so the flag can never be wrong.

RANK, DENSE_RANK or ROW_NUMBER for a top five?

RANK gives ties the same rank and skips numbers (1, 1, 3). DENSE_RANK does not skip (1, 1, 2). ROW_NUMBER gives every row a different number and breaks ties at random. For "top five vacancies" RANK is the fair choice, and you say that ties may return more than five rows.

Why COUNT(DISTINCT ...) in the funnel?

Joining interview results multiplies rows: an applicant with two interviews appears twice. Counting distinct application ids counts each application once per stage.

Why index foreign key columns?

Joins and filters use them all the time, and deleting a parent row has to search the child table. PostgreSQL does not index them for you, so you add the index yourself.

Why audit with a trigger instead of in the application code?

The trigger fires for every update, from the API, a script, or a DBA at the console, so nothing escapes the log. It runs inside the same transaction, so if the update rolls back, the audit row does too.

Why store a password hash and not the password?

If the database leaks, a slow salted hash such as bcrypt cannot be turned back into the password. The application hashes the password at registration and compares hashes at login; the database never sees the real password.

Before: TABLE ACCESS FULL on APPLICATIONS. After: INDEX RANGE SCAN on IDX_APP_VACANCY followed by TABLE ACCESS BY INDEX ROWID. On a table this small Oracle may still choose the full scan, because reading 15 rows is cheaper than using an index. That is the right choice; the index pays off as the table grows.

Interview questions

Why is "one application per applicant per vacancy" a UNIQUE constraint and not a check in the API?

Two requests can arrive at the same moment, and both API checks would pass. A UNIQUE on (applicant_id, vacancy_id) is enforced by the database itself, so the second insert always fails. The API can still check first to show a friendly message.

Why does the average per vacancy use a LEFT JOIN?

An inner join drops vacancies with no applications, so they would vanish from the average and make it look higher. The LEFT JOIN keeps them with a count of 0. The status filter must sit in the ON, or a WHERE would remove those rows again.

How would you fix vacancies that are still Open after closing?

Close them with UPDATE vacancies SET status = 'Closed' WHERE status = 'Open' AND closing_date < TRUNC(SYSDATE);, and run it every night as a DBMS_SCHEDULER job. Better still, compute "open" from the dates when you read, so the flag can never be wrong.

RANK, DENSE_RANK or ROW_NUMBER for a top five?

RANK gives ties the same rank and skips numbers (1, 1, 3). DENSE_RANK does not skip (1, 1, 2). ROW_NUMBER gives every row a different number and breaks ties at random. For "top five vacancies" RANK is the fair choice, and you say that ties may return more than five rows.

Why COUNT(DISTINCT ...) in the funnel?

Joining interview results multiplies rows: an applicant with two interviews appears twice. Counting distinct application ids counts each application once per stage.

Why index foreign key columns?

Joins and filters use them all the time, and deleting a parent row has to search the child table. Oracle does not index them for you, so you add the index yourself.

Why audit with a trigger instead of in the application code?

The trigger fires for every update, from the API, a script, or a DBA at the console, so nothing escapes the log. It runs inside the same transaction, so if the update rolls back, the audit row does too.

Why store a password hash and not the password?

If the database leaks, a slow salted hash such as bcrypt cannot be turned back into the password. The application hashes the password at registration and compares hashes at login; the database never sees the real password.

Interview questions

Why is "one application per applicant per vacancy" a UNIQUE constraint and not a check in the API?

Two requests can arrive at the same moment, and both API checks would pass. A UNIQUE on (applicant_id, vacancy_id) is enforced by the database itself, so the second insert always fails. The API can still check first to show a friendly message.

Why does the average per vacancy use a LEFT JOIN?

An inner join drops vacancies with no applications, so they would vanish from the average and make it look higher. The LEFT JOIN keeps them with a count of 0. The status filter must sit in the ON, or a WHERE would remove those rows again.

How would you fix vacancies that are still Open after closing?

Close them with UPDATE vacancies SET status = 'Closed' WHERE status = 'Open' AND closing_date < CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE);, and run it every night as a SQL Server Agent job. Better still, compute "open" from the dates when you read, so the flag can never be wrong.

RANK, DENSE_RANK or ROW_NUMBER for a top five?

RANK gives ties the same rank and skips numbers (1, 1, 3). DENSE_RANK does not skip (1, 1, 2). ROW_NUMBER gives every row a different number and breaks ties at random. For "top five vacancies" RANK is the fair choice, and you say that ties may return more than five rows.

Why COUNT(DISTINCT ...) in the funnel?

Joining interview results multiplies rows: an applicant with two interviews appears twice. Counting distinct application ids counts each application once per stage.

Why index foreign key columns?

Joins and filters use them all the time, and deleting a parent row has to search the child table. SQL Server does not index them for you, so you add the index yourself.

Why audit with a trigger instead of in the application code?

The trigger fires for every update, from the API, a script, or a DBA at the console, so nothing escapes the log. It runs inside the same transaction, so if the update rolls back, the audit row does too.

Why store a password hash and not the password?

If the database leaks, a slow salted hash such as bcrypt cannot be turned back into the password. The application hashes the password at registration and compares hashes at login; the database never sees the real password.

Done Task 1 is complete

You built recruit_db, answered every question on the sheet, and can explain each design choice. Next, try Task 2 with the Question buttons at the top.

Step 1 Read the question and draw the ERD

Task 2, as given.
  1. Draw an ERD with the entities Applicants, Workstations and Assessments.
  2. Create the database and populate each table with at least 10 rows.
  3. Find the most used workstation (Q1) and the workstations never used (Q2). Show every workstation with its usage count, including unused ones (Q3).
  4. Find the average score per workstation (Q4), the highest-scoring applicant (Q5), applicants with no assessment (Q6), applicant, assessment and workstation details together (Q7), and applicants scoring above the overall average (Q8). Produce other join questions too.
  5. Q9: create a view that hides sensitive applicant data and shows only what recruitment officers need.
  6. Q10: do a full backup, restore it to another database, and verify that the data and constraints are preserved, secure, scalable and follow the business rules.

Workstations and applicants have a many-to-many relationship: one applicant can use several workstations over time, and one workstation serves many applicants. Assessments is the table in the middle, and it also carries the facts of each sitting: type, date, session and score.

+--------------------+          +----------------------------+          +----------------------+
| APPLICANTS         |          | ASSESSMENTS                |          | WORKSTATIONS         |
+--------------------+          +----------------------------+          +----------------------+
| PK applicant_id    |1        *| PK assessment_id           |*        1| PK workstation_id    |
|    full_name       |----------| FK applicant_id            |----------|    station_code  UQ  |
|    email       UQ  |          | FK workstation_id          |          |    centre_name       |
|    phone           |          |    assessment_type         |          |    room              |
|    national_id UQ  |          |    assessment_date         |          |    status            |
|    date_of_birth   |          |    session_slot            |          +----------------------+
+--------------------+          |    score (0 to 100)        |
                                +----------------------------+
UQ (applicant_id, assessment_type)                   one attempt per test type
UQ (workstation_id, assessment_date, session_slot)   one person per seat per session
Business ruleHow the database enforces it
An applicant is identified by email and National IDUNIQUE (email), UNIQUE (national_id)
A score is between 0 and 100CHECK (score BETWEEN 0 AND 100)
One attempt per assessment typeUNIQUE (applicant_id, assessment_type)
A workstation seats one person per sessionUNIQUE (workstation_id, assessment_date, session_slot)
Every assessment belongs to a real applicant and workstationTwo FOREIGN KEYs
Officers never see National IDs, birth dates or emailsA view plus GRANT SELECT on the view only

Step 9 Explain it: secure, scalable, business rules

How do you show that the restored database is "secure"?

The officer still has SELECT on the view and nothing on the tables, so National IDs and birth dates stay hidden. Log in as the officer: the view works and SELECT * FROM applicants; fails. MySQL accounts are server-wide ('recruit_officer'@'localhost'), so they are not in the dump. On a new server, create the account and the grant again.

How is the design "scalable"?

Identity keys never collide, every foreign key column leads an index (through the two composite unique constraints), and the date column has its own index. Reports join on indexed integer keys, so they stay fast as the tables grow.

How do you prove the business rules still hold after a restore?

You try to break each one and expect an error: a duplicate email, a double-booked seat, a score out of range and a missing applicant. A restore that silently lost a constraint is caught at once.

Why is assessments the table in the middle?

Applicants and workstations are many-to-many. A relational database stores that with a junction table, and here the junction table also holds the facts of each sitting: type, date, session and score.

Why does Q2 use LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL and not NOT IN?

NOT IN returns no rows at all if the subquery ever contains a NULL. The LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL pattern, or NOT EXISTS, has no such trap.

Is a view enough to hide data?

No. A view only chooses columns. The hiding works because the officer is granted the view and denied the tables. For stronger protection add column-level privileges, row-level security, or masking at the database level.
